pollination.notes: Approximate group, from NFC flowering records (mid-season).

climate.best_climates: Drier, shallower soils of the Welsh border country; old writers found it at home even in poor hedgerow ground.
climate.poor_climates: Exposed, windy sites where blossom is damaged; untested in hot or very cold climates.

health.other: Disease record not documented; main recorded weakness is alternate cropping and wind-damaged blossom.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage tree for collectors: shelter it from cold spring winds and expect alternate-year crops. Use the fruit for baking and drying as well as a light cider.

varieties.name: George Cave
varieties.history: Raised in 1923 by George Cave at Dovercourt, near Harwich. The Essex nursery Seabrook & Sons took it up and named it after him in 1945; it remains one of the most reliable very early English eaters.

look.description: Medium, slightly ribbed apple, greenish-yellow with a bright red flush and stripes on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Juicy, fine-textured white flesh with a sharp but pleasant, zingy flavour, stronger than most early apples though without the aromatic depth of later ones. Crisp only on the day it is picked: it softens within hours and goes dry and mealy within days.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, on the day of picking

tree.notes: Partly tip-bearing and a regular cropper; fruit drops quickly once ripe, so pick over several days.

pollination.notes: Early flowering (usually listed group 2, sometimes 3); partly self-fertile, with frost-tolerant blossom.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate Britain, including colder and more northerly gardens, since it ripens early and its blossom tolerates frost.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would make the quick-softening fruit go mealy even sooner.

health.other: No major weaknesses recorded and considered suitable for organic growing; main drawback is very short keeping and pre-harvest drop.

varieties.grow_notes: A good first apple of the season for a garden. Plant with another early-flowering variety and check the tree daily in August, as ripe fruit falls readily.

varieties.name: George Neal
varieties.history: Raised in 1904 by Mrs Reeves at Otford in Kent and introduced in 1923 by R. Neal & Sons of Wandsworth, London, receiving an RHS Award of Merit the same year.

look.description: Large, flat, ribbed apple, pale green-yellow with a light pinkish flush and stripes.

taste.summary: Rather soft, coarse, juicy greenish flesh with a clean acidity; cooks quickly, collapsing almost completely into a smooth purée.

tree.notes: Little modern growing data recorded.

pollination.notes: Among the earliest to flower in the National Fruit Collection records, consistent with group 2; pair with another early bloomer.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate south-east England, where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: Early flowering makes it vulnerable in frost pockets; untested in hot climates.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: An early-season cooker for southern gardens. Avoid frost pockets because it blooms early, and use the fruit from August onwards for purées and sauces.

varieties.name: Gladstone

origin.place: Worcestershire, England (rediscovered at Blakedown Nursery, Kidderminster)

varieties.history: Thought to date from around 1780; it was rediscovered by Mr Jackson of Blakedown Nursery near Kidderminster and sold from 1868 as 'Jackson's Seedling'. After an RHS First Class Certificate in 1883 it was renamed in honour of the Prime Minister W. E. Gladstone.

look.description: Conical, somewhat ribbed apple, mostly covered with a dark red flush and stripes over greenish yellow.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy when just picked, with a sweet, pleasantly aromatic flavour, but it turns soft and slightly floury within a few days.
taste.best_eaten: late Jul-Aug, straight from the tree

tree.notes: Fairly vigorous, partly tip-bearing tree that starts cropping young and bears heavily and regularly.

pollination.notes: Listed in group 4 and partly self-fertile; blossom has some frost resistance.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild, damp temperate climates such as the English Midlands and west.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers would make the very early, quick-softening fruit mealy almost at once.

health.other: Reported to be very resistant to scab and canker; its weakness is that the fruit keeps only a few days.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the earliest English eating apples, best for gardeners who will eat it straight off the tree. Pick little and often as the fruit colours, as it does not keep.

varieties.name: Glockenapfel

origin.place: Uncertain: usually linked to Switzerland, possibly southern Germany or the Altes Land on the lower Elbe

varieties.history: A chance seedling that appeared around the middle of the 19th century; Switzerland, southern Germany and the Altes Land fruit district near Hamburg are all suggested as its birthplace. Named for its tall bell shape, it became an important late-keeping apple in Switzerland and northern Germany and is a traditional choice for strudel.

look.description: Tall, bell-shaped, ribbed fruit with a smooth greenish-yellow skin, dark dots and sometimes a faint orange-red cheek.

taste.summary: Very firm, pale flesh, not very juicy, with pronounced, slightly harsh acidity and a strong aroma. Picked in October but not ready to eat until about December, and keeps around six months; it barely breaks down when cooked, making it a classic strudel and pie apple. One grower found it mild and only lightly sweet.

tree.notes: Vigorous when young, settling to moderate growth with a characteristic drooping habit; branches tend to become bare inside, so regular renewal pruning helps. Standard trees tend to alternate, and young wood can be frost-damaged after a heavy crop.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly early (well before Cox at Brogdale). Described in German sources as partly self-fertile and a good pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist fruit districts of Switzerland, southern and northern Germany with a long growing season and fertile soil.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed sites where wood is frost-damaged, and dry or poor soils that reduce fruit quality.

health.other: Low scab susceptibility but occasionally cankers; prone to bare wood and to frost damage in young shoots after heavy crops.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a warm, sheltered spot on moist, fertile soil and thin the crop to reduce alternate bearing. Pick in mid October and store cold; it is one of the longest-keeping cooking apples.

varieties.name: Gloster

origin.place: Obstbauversuchsanstalt Jork, Altes Land, near Hamburg, Germany
origin.parentage: Glockenapfel (Weisser Winterglockenapfel) x Richared Delicious

varieties.history: Crossed in 1951 at the fruit research station at Jork in the Altes Land fruit region near Hamburg and released in 1969, hence the alternative name Gloster 69. It was planted commercially in northern Germany and the Low Countries as a long-keeping red apple.

look.description: Tall, bell-shaped fruit with Delicious-like bumps at the eye, almost wholly covered in dark purplish red with prominent lenticels.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp and juicy greenish-cream flesh with a fairly sharp flavour, tarter than Delicious, finishing with a hint of honey according to one grower. Hangs well on the tree, keeps its crunch for months and mellows slightly in store.

tree.notes: Undemanding but needs deep soil for good yields. Fruit hangs firmly and resists wind; wood and blossom show little frost damage.

pollination.notes: German sources give early-to-mid May flowering; no UK flowering group found. Plant with a mid-season partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool northern European lowlands such as the Altes Land and the Low Countries, where it colours well and stores into spring.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with fire blight or cedar-apple rust pressure (much of the eastern US) need regular control; probably less well coloured in warm-night climates.

health.other: Susceptible to fire blight and cedar-apple rust; moderately to highly scab-prone; long-stored fruit can develop core rot.

varieties.grow_notes: Best on deep, moisture-retentive soil in an open site. Pick at full colour in October and store cool; watch for scab in wet springs.

varieties.name: Golden Bounty

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Emneth Early (Early Victoria)

varieties.history: Raised around 1940 by A.C. Nash at Scutes Farm, Hastings, from Cox crossed with the early cooker Emneth Early. A Sussex local variety now kept in the National Fruit Collection and the Brighton Permaculture Trust's Sussex collection at Stanmer Park.

look.description: Yellow apple marked with fine, broken orange and red stripes and a little russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, crisp flesh with a rich, brisk, sharply aromatic flavour that recalls an early-season Cox with extra acidity.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and heavy-cropping; other habits not recorded.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from Brogdale flowering records, which match Cox.

climate.best_climates: South-east England and similar mild temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented beyond southern England; estimates are inferred from its parents.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A Sussex heritage apple for a sunny southern garden. Pick in mid-September, eat within a few weeks, and pair with a group 2-4 pollinator.

varieties.name: Golden Delicious

origin.place: Anderson Mullins farm, Clay County, West Virginia
origin.parentage: Chance seedling; often said to be Grimes Golden x Golden Reinette, but unproven
origin.raised_by: Found by Anderson Mullins; introduced by Stark Bros

varieties.history: A chance seedling that appeared on the Mullins family farm in West Virginia around the 1890s. Stark Bros Nurseries bought the tree in 1914 and launched it in 1916; it became one of the world's most planted apples and a parent of Gala, Jonagold, Elstar, Mutsu and many others.

look.description: Long-stalked, slightly conical apple, green-yellow ripening to clear golden-yellow, sometimes with a faint pink cheek; prone to fine russet netting in damp climates.

taste.summary: Left to ripen to golden-green on the tree it is crisp, juicy and richly sweet, with a honeyed, pear-drop note and only modest acidity; a few tasters also pick up a faint ginger or cinnamon warmth. Fruit picked green and held in long storage is the bland, soft, crumbly supermarket apple. Holds its shape when cooked.

tree.notes: Easy, precocious spur-bearer with wide-angled branches; crops heavily and needs thinning to keep fruit size and annual bearing.

pollination.notes: Group 4, partly self-fertile, and an excellent pollen donor for other diploids.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sunny temperate climates with long seasons (Washington, northern Italy, southern France, Chile), where it ripens to a rich golden colour.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, damp regions such as much of Britain give greener, blander fruit with skin russet; very humid areas bring heavy scab and rust.

health.other: Susceptible to scab, powdery mildew and cedar-apple rust; skin bruises and shrivels easily, and damp springs cause russeting.

varieties.grow_notes: Reliable and productive, but in Britain it needs a warm, sunny site to taste good. Thin crops, pick only when the ground colour turns yellow, and store in plastic bags in a cold place to limit shrivelling.

varieties.name: Golden Delicious Russet

origin.parentage: Presumed russeted sport or selection of Golden Delicious (not verified)

varieties.history: No independent pomological record of this name was found. The name points to a russet-skinned form of Golden Delicious; several russeted sports of Golden Delicious are known (for example Razor Russet from Kentucky), but which one is sold under this name could not be confirmed. Values below assume it behaves like Golden Delicious.

look.description: Golden Delicious-shaped yellow apple with extensive brownish russet over the skin (extent unverified).

taste.summary: Expected to taste like Golden Delicious: sweet, honeyed and low in acid, with the slightly richer, drier mouthfeel that russeted skin often brings. Not independently described.

tree.notes: Assumed to grow like Golden Delicious: precocious, heavy-cropping spur-bearer.

pollination.notes: Golden Delicious is group 4 and partly self-fertile; assumed the same.

climate.best_climates: If it is a Golden Delicious sport, warm temperate regions with long sunny autumns suit it best.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short British seasons can leave late Golden Delicious types under-ripe and bland.

health.other: Not recorded for this name; Golden Delicious itself is prone to scab, mildew and cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Treat as Golden Delicious: a warm, sunny site and a long season help, and it is a useful group 4 pollinator. Check the supplier's description of origin before relying on these assumed traits.

varieties.name: Golden Hornet

origin.parentage: Unknown; usually grouped under Malus x zumi

varieties.history: Introduced around the late 1940s by the Waterer nursery firm in southern England. It became one of Britain's most widely planted ornamental crabs and orchard pollinators; it held the RHS Award of Garden Merit until 2013.

look.description: Small egg- to cone-shaped fruits about 2-2.5 cm, ripening clear golden-yellow and packed thickly along the branches, where they hang on into early winter.

taste.summary: Sharp and somewhat astringent raw with little flavour of its own. Used mainly as a pectin-rich base for jelly, which comes out golden rather than red.

tree.notes: Upright when young, opening out and getting a little straggly with age; about 3-5 m after ten years on a semi-vigorous stock. Heavy crops can weigh branches down.

pollination.notes: White blossom from pink-tinged buds. Nursery sources place it anywhere in groups 3-5, so it overlaps most mid- and late-flowering apples and is a standard pollinator in British orchards.

climate.best_climates: Mild temperate maritime climates such as the UK and north-west Europe, where the yellow fruit display lasts well into winter.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid districts encourage scab; warm, humid summers raise the risk of fire blight.

health.other: Some scab in wet seasons and some susceptibility to fire blight where that disease occurs. Lost its RHS Award of Garden Merit in 2013.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a sunny, open spot so the foliage dries quickly and scab stays down. Pick fruit for jelly before it starts to fall, and plant it near mid- or late-flowering apples to earn its keep as a pollinator.

varieties.name: Golden Knob
varieties.history: An old English apple that the National Fruit Collection traces to Enmore Castle in Somerset, in cultivation since the late 1700s. The synonym Kentish Golden Knob points to its later popularity in Kent; a different, unrelated 'Golden Knob' from Berkshire is also recorded.

look.description: Small, flattish, unribbed apple, greenish-yellow with a faint brownish flush and some russet.

taste.summary: Firm, very fine-textured white flesh with a sweet, nutty flavour; a small late-keeping dessert apple in the russet-like style.

tree.notes: Little modern growing data.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded; plant with a mid-season diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Southern English lowlands from Somerset to Kent, where it has been grown for over two centuries.
climate.poor_climates: No records from hot or very cold climates.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage keeper for collectors. Pick in mid-October, store somewhere cool and slightly humid, and pair it with a mid-season flowering diploid.

varieties.name: Golden Noble

origin.place: Stow Bardolph (Stow Hall), near Downham Market, Norfolk, England

varieties.history: Found by Patrick Flanagan, head gardener to Sir Thomas Hare at Stow Hall in Norfolk, in an old orchard there. William Forsyth mentioned it in 1803 and Flanagan presented it to the Horticultural Society of London in 1820; it is a parent of Edward VII.

look.description: Large, clear golden-yellow apple without a flush, sometimes with scattered russet dots.

taste.summary: Juicy, fairly fine cream flesh with a bright acidity that has enough sweetness to need little sugar; cooks into a smooth, golden, well-flavoured purée.

tree.notes: Neat, tidy growth that suits a garden; comes into bearing early and crops regularly.

pollination.notes: Usually listed in group 4 (one database says 5); blossom is somewhat frost-sensitive.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate lowland England, especially drier eastern counties like its native Norfolk.
climate.poor_climates: Frost-prone sites can damage its blossom; hot, humid areas would add mildew and fire blight pressure.

health.other: Fair resistance to scab and canker, but quite prone to powdery mildew and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the finest cookers for a small garden thanks to its neat habit. Avoid the lowest frost pockets, keep mildew in check by pruning out infected shoots, and pick from late September.

varieties.name: Golden Russet
aka: Golden Russet of Western New York

origin.parentage: Chance seedling, thought to come from an English russet (sometimes said to be English Golden Russet); unconfirmed

varieties.history: A New York russet that was in circulation by the first half of the nineteenth century and became a farmhouse favourite for winter storage. It has had a second life with the revival of American craft cider, where its very high sugar content makes it one of the most sought-after cider fruits.

look.description: Small to medium, slightly squat fruit almost entirely coated in golden-bronze russet, occasionally with a faint coppery-orange cheek.

taste.summary: Dense, fine-grained, crisp flesh with intense sugar balanced by lively acidity; nutty and rich, with some tasters noting a hint of pear and a spiced, cider-like depth. Sharp early in the season, it sweetens markedly in store but loses crispness after a month or two.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Feb; sweeter after a few weeks in store

tree.notes: A vigorous tree that one widely used database lists as tip-bearing and a regular, good cropper; avoid heavy spur pruning and renew fruiting wood instead.

pollination.notes: Recorded as an early-flowering (group 2) diploid in one database; needs a compatible partner flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental climates such as New York, New England, the Great Lakes and eastern Canada, where a long, sunny autumn concentrates sugar.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, sunless summers leave the fruit sharp and undersized; very hot, humid regions favour fire blight and rust.

health.other: Fairly scab-tolerant, but susceptible to fire blight and somewhat to cedar-apple rust. Russeted skin shrivels in dry storage, so keep it humid.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil and give it a few years to settle into cropping. Because it tends to fruit at shoot tips, prune lightly by renewal. Store in a humid cellar or bag to prevent shrivelling.

varieties.name: Golden Spire

origin.raised_by: Richard Smith of Worcester (finder and introducer)

varieties.history: A Victorian apple found in Lancashire around 1850 and put into commerce by the Worcester nurseryman Richard Smith. It later spread into Gloucestershire, where it went by the name Tom Matthews and was used in cider making as well as in the kitchen.

look.description: Tall, narrow, strongly ribbed fruit, greenish-yellow ripening to gold, with at most a few faint orange streaks.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, juicy cream flesh; sharp, with a slightly astringent, distinctly cider-like back-taste, though tasters find enough sweetness to eat it fresh straight from the tree. Cooks down to a well-flavoured purée; it is not a keeper and is best used early.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing. Generally regular, though old trees are reported to fall into alternate heavy and light years. Blossom is showy and early.

pollination.notes: Flowers early (NFC records it opening with Keswick Codlin); Orange Pippin places it in group 1 and calls it self-fertile, but a group 1-3 partner will improve cropping. A good pollen donor.

climate.best_climates: Cool, damp northern and western British conditions such as its native Lancashire and the cider country of Gloucestershire.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or continental climates; as an early, sharp English apple it is likely to soften and drop early in hot summers.

health.other: Rated about average for disease; somewhat susceptible to scab. Wasps attack ripe fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, attractive tree for northern or wet gardens that wants a dual-purpose cooking and cider apple. Plant with an early-flowering partner and use the fruit within a few weeks of picking.

varieties.name: Goldrush

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Co-op 17 (a PRI scab-resistant selection with Malus floribunda in its ancestry)

varieties.history: Bred in the joint disease-resistance programme of Purdue, Rutgers and the University of Illinois, which aimed for apples that need no scab sprays. Tested as Co-op 38 and released in the early 1990s, it has become a favourite of organic and backyard growers for its keeping quality and immunity to scab.

look.description: Greenish-yellow apple that turns deep gold in store, sometimes with a faint bronze-orange cheek and a little russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Very hard and crisp, with high sugar and high acid at the same time. Straight off the tree it can be harshly sharp; after a month or two in store it mellows into an intense, spicy sweet-tart apple with a long, rich finish, and it keeps its crunch for months.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Apr; too sharp at picking, best after 1-3 months in store

tree.notes: Willowy branches bend under heavy crops. Strongly inclined to alternate bearing and to small fruit if left unthinned, so thin hard and early in an 'on' year. Needs a long season; fruit hangs well on the tree.

pollination.notes: Mid-late flowering diploid; plant with another group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Places with long, warm summers and long autumns, such as the US Midwest, mid-Atlantic and upper South, where it ripens fully and develops its best sugar.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or cool maritime areas (northern Britain, high latitudes) where it may not ripen before winter; humid areas with junipers need rust control.

health.other: Immune to the common races of scab (Vf gene) and fairly tolerant of mildew, but notably susceptible to cedar-apple rust. Main cultural problems are biennial bearing and undersized fruit on overcropped trees.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice where spraying is unwelcome, as long as the site gives a long, warm autumn; in Britain it suits the south-east on a sunny wall or open site. Thin fruit to one per cluster to keep size up and to even out cropping, and pick as late as frost allows.

varieties.name: Goodland

origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of Patten Greening

varieties.history: Raised at the Morden station in Manitoba from a seedling of the hardy Iowa apple Patten Greening and released in the mid-20th century (Orange Pippin places it in the 1940s). It became a standard dessert and sauce apple for prairie gardens.

look.description: Roundish pale yellow apple with a red blush.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy with a sweet, gently tart flavour and a pleasant aroma; good fresh and cooks down to a smooth sauce.

tree.notes: Productive, and usually fruiting within about four years of planting.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded; plant another hardy apple or crab nearby.

climate.best_climates: Prairie and northern continental gardens with very cold winters and short, warm summers.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer or mild-winter regions; like most prairie apples it is likely to ripen soft there and may lack chill.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good first apple for cold northern gardens. Plant in full sun with a hardy pollinator and thin the crop in heavy years to keep fruit size up.

varieties.name: Gordon
varieties.history: A southern California apple from Whittier, in the Los Angeles basin, grown in home orchards for its low chill need and its long, drawn-out flowering and ripening. Its parentage and date are not well recorded.

look.description: Reported as green to yellow-green with red stripes and flush; fuller details not verified.

taste.summary: Described by Californian growers as crisp and juicy with a sweet-tart flavour, good both fresh and cooked; detailed tasting data are scarce.
taste.best_eaten: Through its long picking season (Aug-Oct in California)

tree.notes: Vigorous, upright tree with an unusually long bloom period, so it overlaps with many other varieties; fruit ripens over several weeks, which suits home growers.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded. Its long bloom makes it a useful partner for other low-chill apples.

climate.best_climates: Mild-winter, warm-summer regions such as coastal and inland southern California, where it ripens from August into October with about 400 chill hours.
climate.poor_climates: Cold-winter regions where early blossom is frosted, and cool short summers that cannot ripen its long-season crop.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good backyard apple for mild-winter gardens, where its long bloom and staggered ripening spread the harvest. Give it room or prune hard, as it grows vigorously.

varieties.name: Granny Smith

origin.place: Eastwood, Ryde, Sydney, New South Wales
origin.parentage: Chance seedling, traditionally said to come from discarded French Crab apples; the other parent is unknown

varieties.history: Arose as a chance seedling on the orchard of Maria Ann Smith, an English emigrant from Sussex, near Sydney; trees were fruiting by 1868. Its long keeping and ability to ship made it one of the world's main export apples in the 20th century.

look.description: Bright grass-green apple with conspicuous pale lenticel dots, occasionally a faint brownish-pink cheek and a little fine russet near the stalk.

taste.summary: Hard, crisp and juicy with a clean, sharp, lemony acidity and only moderate sweetness; flavour is simple rather than aromatic. Sweetens a little and yellows in store. Cooks well, keeping some shape and plenty of tang.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Apr; UK-grown fruit needs a long warm autumn to ripen properly

tree.notes: Partial tip-bearer, so avoid shortening all the young laterals. Crops heavily and early; thin to keep fruit size.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records show it flowering alongside Cox and Golden Delicious; some lists put it a group later. Partly self-fertile but sets better with a partner.

climate.best_climates: Warm-temperate and Mediterranean climates with long, hot growing seasons: Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Chile, California, southern Europe and Washington State.
climate.poor_climates: Cool short-summer areas such as northern Britain and Scandinavia, where it often fails to ripen and stays hard, sour and starchy.

health.other: Susceptible to scab, powdery mildew and fire blight; fruit prone to superficial scald in store and to sunburn in very hot climates.

varieties.grow_notes: Only worth growing in Britain on a warm, sheltered south-facing site where it can hang into November. Elsewhere it is easy and productive in warm climates; spray or choose a clean site for scab and mildew, and thin heavily.

varieties.name: Gravenstein

origin.place: Gråsten (Gravenstein), South Jutland; possibly brought there from Italy or Germany

varieties.history: Grown at Gråsten castle in Schleswig by the late 1600s, though it may have come from Italy or Germany; Denmark named it its national apple in 2005. Russian settlers took it to Fort Ross in California in the early 1800s and it later became the signature apple of Sonoma County and of Nova Scotia's Annapolis Valley.

look.description: Large, lumpy, somewhat flattened fruit, yellow-green streaked and splashed with orange-red; a fully red sport also exists.

taste.summary: Juicy, crisp and highly aromatic when fresh, with a lively sweet-sharp balance; one of the most perfumed early apples. It softens within days of picking and makes outstanding sauce, pies and juice.

tree.notes: Makes a very large tree with thick dark leaves; slow to start bearing and inclined to biennial cropping. Fruit ripens unevenly and drops, so several pickings are needed.

pollination.notes: Triploid and a poor pollen donor; very early flowering (group 1, some lists group 2), so it needs two early-flowering diploid partners and is at risk from spring frost.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist maritime or coastal climates: Denmark and northern Germany, coastal Sonoma County, Nova Scotia, the Pacific Northwest.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, dry interior summers and very harsh continental winters; early bloom suffers in frost-prone sites.

health.other: Very susceptible to fire blight; early blossom is frost-prone, and fruit keeps only a week or two.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it plenty of room, deep moist loam and a frost-free site, and plant two early-flowering pollinators. Pick over several passes and use the fruit quickly.

varieties.name: Greensleeves

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: James Grieve x Golden Delicious
origin.raised_by: Dr F.H. Alston, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Bred in 1966 by Dr Alston at East Malling from James Grieve and Golden Delicious and released in the 1970s as a reliable, compact garden apple. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Smooth, round, pale green apple ripening to yellow-green, with no blush.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy with a clean, refreshing tang when picked early; it mellows to a milder, sweeter apple in store.

tree.notes: Compact, very precocious and prolific; thin hard to keep fruit size and avoid alternate cropping. Well suited to small gardens and trained forms.

pollination.notes: Group 3 and partly self-fertile; a good pollinator for other mid-season apples.

climate.best_climates: Throughout Britain and north-west Europe, including cooler and more northerly gardens.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers soften the fruit and flatten its fresh acidity.

health.other: Reasonably healthy for a garden apple; heavy crops need thinning.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy first apple tree for a small garden, cordon or patio pot. Thin fruitlets in June and pick some early for a sharper taste.

varieties.name: Grenadier
varieties.history: Thought to come from Buckinghamshire; first noted in 1862, it reached the trade around 1875 and gained an RHS First Class Certificate in 1883. It became the main early-season commercial cooking apple in Britain and still holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Big, ribbed, broadly conical apple with smooth, rather greasy pale green skin, occasionally with a faint brownish tinge.

taste.summary: Firm, fine white flesh, juicy and sharply acid, though fully ripe fruit is almost sweet enough to eat raw. In the pan it collapses quickly into a pale, creamy, tart purée with a fine, heady apple scent, ideal for sauce and early-season pies; it keeps only a week or so.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Sep, straight from the tree; does not keep

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and fairly compact; crops young, heavily and regularly. Partly tip-bearing, so leave some one-year tips when pruning. The fruit bruises easily.

pollination.notes: Mid-season blossom and a good pollinator for other group 2-4 diploids; partly self-fertile.

climate.best_climates: Throughout Britain, including the cooler, wetter north and west and higher ground; a dependable choice for maritime temperate climates.
climate.poor_climates: Very hot summers would ripen it even earlier and shorten its already brief season; little record outside temperate Europe.

health.other: Generally healthy and tolerant of poor growing conditions; fruit bruises and does not store.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the easiest cookers for beginners and for cold or exposed gardens. Pick from mid-August as soon as fruit is large enough and use within a couple of weeks.

varieties.name: Grimes Golden

origin.raised_by: Found on the farm of Thomas Grimes

varieties.history: A chance seedling on Thomas Grimes's farm in the northern panhandle of West Virginia, propagated from the early 1800s. It is widely accepted as a parent of Golden Delicious and remains a respected dessert and cider apple in the Appalachian region.

look.description: Clear golden-yellow apple with conspicuous pale lenticels and light russet flecks, on a long stalk.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, fine-grained yellow-white flesh with a rich, sweet and noticeably spicy flavour, fuller than its offspring Golden Delicious, with a clean, dry finish; one taster also notes a slight pear flavour. Keeps into February; good fresh and in pies, sauce, apple butter and cider.

tree.notes: Comes into bearing fairly young. Prone to collar rot, so avoid wet, heavy soils and plant the graft union well above ground.

pollination.notes: Reported as partly self-fertile, but crops better with a partner in groups 2-4; a good pollen donor.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer Appalachian and mid-Atlantic districts with long autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, heavy soils (collar rot) and short, cool seasons that do not develop its full sweetness.

health.other: Collar rot (Phytophthora) is the main weakness; otherwise moderately disease-resistant.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose a well-drained site and avoid waterlogged ground because of collar rot. Pick when the skin turns from green to gold; it shrivels if left too long in a dry store.

varieties.name: Gyllenkroks Astrakan
varieties.history: Believed to have arisen in the 18th century on the Regnaholm estate in Östergötland and named after the Gyllenkrok family who owned it. The Alnarp nursery began selling it in 1902, and it is now the provincial apple of Östergötland.

look.description: Round, just under medium-sized pale greenish-yellow fruit striped with red.

taste.summary: Loose-textured, juicy early apple of good flavour, best eaten straight from the tree; like other summer apples it does not keep.

tree.notes: Makes a medium-sized, not very vigorous tree that crops early and well. Fruit ripens over a period and should be picked in several rounds when fully ripe.

pollination.notes: Pollination details not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cool continental Scandinavia; recommended in Swedish growing zones I-IV.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented in warm climates; as a Nordic summer apple it is unlikely to suit hot summers.

health.other: Fungal disease occurs but less than in other Astrakan-type apples; generally easy and undemanding. Harvest date for south-east England estimated from the Swedish early-September picking.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, early-cropping summer apple for cold gardens. Pick in stages as fruits ripen and eat them promptly.

varieties.name: Hagloe Crab

origin.place: Hagloe, parish of Awre, near Blakeney, Gloucestershire, England
origin.parentage: Seedling of unknown parentage (not a true crab apple)

varieties.history: Said by William Marshall to have been raised from seed around 1720 on the Bellamy family's land at Hagloe in the Forest of Dean; Knight suspected it was older. Its cider was among the most prized of the eighteenth century, fetching extraordinary prices, but the variety almost vanished; graftwood from a verified old tree at Tibberton now survives in the Gloucestershire Apple Collection, and it is critically rare.

look.description: Small, oblong-ovate, lop-sided fruit, pale yellow to green with broken bright red streaks, orange where thin, and a net of russet over much of the skin.

taste.summary: The flesh is firm and dry, sweet with a bitter edge; old analyses describe sweetish, subacid juice with some astringency, and harshness unless fully ripe. Its cider was famed for strength, body and richness when grown on warm limestone soils. Not formally classed: one modern list calls it a sharp, which old descriptions do not support.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill when fully ripe in Nov

tree.notes: Historically described as seldom very productive. Its decline is thought to stem from virus build-up during propagation.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Warm, dry sites on limestone soils with warm autumns, as in its Forest of Dean home.
climate.poor_climates: Deep, rich or heavy vale soils and cool seasons, where the cider stays harsh and rough.

health.other: Light cropping; old stock likely virus-affected.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on a warm, free-draining, ideally limestone site and let the fruit ripen fully before milling. A conservation variety; source from the Gloucestershire collection where possible.

varieties.name: Hambledon Deux Ans
varieties.history: An eighteenth-century Hampshire apple from the village of Hambledon, dating to around 1750. The French-style name boasts of its keeping power ('two years'), and it travelled widely under a long list of local names, several of which wrongly link it to Blenheim Orange.

look.description: Large, flattish-conical apple, greenish-yellow with a dull red flush broken into stripes.

taste.summary: Very firm, coarse and rather dry greenish flesh with a little sweetness, gentle acidity and a faint aroma. Used for cooking through the winter, it mellows enough by spring to be eaten raw.
taste.best_eaten: Jan-Apr for cooking; raw from about Mar

tree.notes: Few modern growing records; old accounts describe a hardy tree. Treat as a standard spur-bearer until it shows otherwise.

pollination.notes: Group estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates, which are close to Bramley's Seedling; plant near a mid-season diploid.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions with a long autumn so the fruit can mature fully before picking in October.
climate.poor_climates: No documented use in hot climates; short northern seasons may not ripen it well enough to store.

health.other: Prone to bitter pit in store; other disease behaviour poorly recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Worth growing purely as a very long keeper to fill the late-winter and spring gap. Feed and water evenly and consider calcium sprays to limit bitter pit; pick in early October and store cool.

varieties.name: Hamid's Red Pippin

origin.place: Keepers Nursery, East Farleigh, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of Rajka; the raiser thinks Discovery was the pollen parent

varieties.history: Raised by Karim Habibi at Keepers Nursery from a pip of the Czech variety Rajka and named for his father Hamid, who ran the nursery from 1993 until 2019. It was one of the first varieties from the nursery's seedling programme, which began with 150 seeds sown in 2014-15.

look.description: Medium, round and almost completely red, with a little russet round the stalk.

taste.summary: A sweet, fruity apple with a light pear-drop note and a crisp, light texture. Tasters compare it with Discovery, but later in the season and stronger in flavour.

tree.notes: Healthy, average-vigour spur-bearer; still a young variety with limited growing history.

pollination.notes: Group 3 (C in nursery lists) on two sources.

climate.best_climates: Raised and tested in Kent; expected to suit temperate British conditions.
climate.poor_climates: Untested outside south-east England.

health.other: Healthy in trials so far; ratings not yet published.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in a sunny spot on well-drained soil with a group 2-4 pollinator. As a new variety, expect limited long-term information on vigour and disease.

varieties.name: Haralson

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of Malinda; DNA evidence points to Wealthy as the pollen parent.

varieties.history: Selected in 1913 among Malinda seedlings at the University of Minnesota's fruit breeding farm and released in 1922, named after the farm superintendent Charles Haralson. It was long Minnesota's most widely planted apple and is a parent of Honeygold.

look.description: Round-conical apple largely covered in glossy red over yellow-green, with prominent pale lenticels.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp and juicy with a distinctly tart, fairly complex flavour that mellows a little in store. Holds its shape when baked, which made it the Upper Midwest's standard pie apple.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Feb; tart at picking, more balanced after a month or two in store

tree.notes: Fairly small tree with a strong central leader and wide-angled laterals. Prone to alternate bearing and to undersized fruit when overloaded, so thin early.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin places it in group 3, though Minnesota describes it as relatively late-blooming. Use another hardy diploid such as Honeygold or Wealthy, or a crab.

climate.best_climates: Cold Upper Midwest and prairie-margin climates with crisp autumns, where it colours and stores well.
climate.poor_climates: Warm-summer regions where fruit ripens dull and soft, and mild-winter areas that cannot satisfy its chill need.

health.other: Some scab susceptibility; fairly tolerant of fire blight and cedar-apple rust. Biennial bearing and small fruit on overcropped trees are the main problems.

varieties.grow_notes: A reliable workhorse for very cold gardens. Thin fruit hard in heavy years, give it full sun, and store the crop in a cold cellar or fridge for winter pies.

varieties.name: Harry Baker

origin.raised_by: Reads Nursery (Norfolk); breeding usually credited to Hugh Ermen

varieties.history: A late twentieth-century British crab named after Harry Baker, the long-serving fruit officer at RHS Wisley. It pairs deep pink blossom with large, dark red, red-fleshed fruit that makes a deeply coloured jelly.

look.description: Large for a crab, round, with dark ruby-red skin and red-stained flesh.

taste.summary: Sharp and fairly juicy with red-tinged flesh; rated very good for the kitchen, giving a rich, deep ruby jelly.

tree.notes: A fairly small, spur-bearing tree; young leaves are tinted copper. Good for small gardens wanting both blossom and a jelly crop.

pollination.notes: Intense deep pink to crimson blossom; a good pollinator for mid- to late-flowering apples.

climate.best_climates: Temperate and mild, damp climates such as the UK.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented outside temperate Europe.

health.other: Rated good overall disease resistance by nursery sources.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in full sun to get the best blossom and fruit colour. Pick in early October for jelly, and pair it with mid- or late-flowering dessert apples as a pollinator.

varieties.name: Harry Masters Jersey

origin.parentage: Unknown; sometimes suggested to be a seedling of Yarlington Mill

varieties.history: Raised or selected by Harry Masters, the Yarlington nurseryman who also spread Yarlington Mill, around the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. It became a standard Somerset bittersweet and is rated of vintage quality.

look.description: Conical, mostly covered in a dark red flush and stripes.

taste.summary: A medium-to-full bittersweet with good sugar, low acid and soft but firm tannin; makes a rich, rounded cider with good body.

tree.notes: Fairly weak-growing and early to bear, with a tip-bearing habit and a strong biennial tendency.

pollination.notes: Needs a pollinator flowering in mid season.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates such as Somerset.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season areas where late fruit cannot ripen.

health.other: Some susceptibility to scab; biennial bearing is the main grower complaint.

varieties.grow_notes: Its modest vigour suits a vigorous rootstock or a bush orchard on MM106. Prune lightly as it bears at the tips. Fruit thinning in on-years helps even out cropping.

varieties.name: Hawthornden
varieties.history: Named after Hawthornden near Edinburgh, home of the 17th-century poet William Drummond. Hogg could not trace when it arose: its earliest listing is in the catalogue of the Edinburgh nurserymen Leslie & Anderson (dated about 1780 by the National Fruit Collection), and it reached London's Brompton Park nursery around 1790. It went on to become one of the most widely planted cookers of 19th-century Britain and spread across Europe, collecting German, Czech, Polish and Russian names. It is a different apple from the later New Hawthornden and Winter Hawthornden.

look.description: Medium to fairly large, flattened fruit, often lopsided from one strong rib; smooth pale greenish-yellow skin with a bloom and a faint pinkish-red flush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: A plain, pleasantly sub-acid kitchen apple. Hogg found the white flesh crisp, tender and very juicy, while the National Fruit Collection notes firm, coarse flesh. It was valued for reliability and early use rather than for strong flavour.

tree.notes: Victorian writers praised it as a healthy tree that starts cropping young and bears abundantly on almost any soil. Bunyard saw only moderate growth and a low, flat-headed tree, so it suits a small garden.

pollination.notes: No published group found. Estimated as group 3 because the National Fruit Collection records it in full bloom the same week as Cox and Bramley. Plant a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, short-summer climates such as Scotland and northern England. Its long history in central and eastern Europe also suggests good winter hardiness.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, wet or poorly drained soils, where it is liable to canker. Hot summers are untested.

health.other: Hogg warned that on some soils it cankers and attracts woolly aphid. Other disease responses are not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, early-bearing cooker for northern or exposed gardens. Give it a well-drained site to keep canker at bay, and check for woolly aphid in spring.

varieties.name: Hereford Redstreak

origin.place: Herefordshire, England (traditionally Lord Scudamore's Holme Lacy estate)
origin.parentage: Seedling ('wilding') of unknown parentage; a later tradition says it grew from a French pip
origin.raised_by: Credited to John Scudamore, 1st Viscount Scudamore

varieties.history: The celebrated seventeenth-century cider apple of Herefordshire, first promoted by Lord Scudamore and praised in verse and prose; its cider once sold for the price of fine wine. It declined through the 1700s, was described as given up by 1796 and as no longer propagable by 1811, and Victorian authors considered the true variety extinct. Trees sold under the name today are of uncertain identity; the NFC's 'Improved Redstreak', a bittersharp known from the 1940s, is sometimes offered in its place.

look.description: Historic accounts describe a roundish fruit narrowing to the eye, clear yellow streaked red, deeper red streaks on the sunny side; firm yellow flesh.

taste.summary: Historic sources record very sugary juice (specific gravity near 1.079) and a sweet, rich, well-coloured cider that lacked strength and did not keep well. Its class is disputed: one modern account calls the original a bittersweet, while modern trees bearing the name test as sharp or bittersharp.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; historically milled Oct-Nov

tree.notes: Old writers describe a low, shrubby, ragged and short-lived tree. Its decline is now often blamed on virus build-up through repeated grafting.

pollination.notes: Not recorded for the historic variety.

climate.best_climates: The Herefordshire and Gloucestershire orchard country of its heyday.
climate.poor_climates: No modern climate data; the original may no longer exist.

health.other: Historic loss of vigour and quality, probably viral. Modern trees sold under the name are reported to be somewhat canker-prone.

varieties.grow_notes: Buy only as a heritage curiosity and ask the nursery about its source, since modern 'Herefordshire Redstreak' trees are probably not the original. Treat any tree under this name as a standard mid-season cider apple.

varieties.name: Herring's Pippin

origin.parentage: Unknown; a seedling credited to a Mr Herring

varieties.history: Credited to a Mr Herring of Lincoln and on record from 1908, it was put on the market by Pearson's nursery of Nottingham (1917 by the East of England Apples & Orchards Project's account). Edward Bunyard described it in 1920 from fruit Pearson sent him and noted that the nurseryman rated it very highly.

look.description: Big, somewhat uneven round-conical fruit, pale greenish-yellow under a heavy scarlet to brownish-red flush with streaks; the skin marks and bruises easily.

taste.summary: Juicy, moderately firm but rather coarse cream flesh with a pronounced spicy, aromatic character that some tasters liken to aniseed. Tart enough to cook, when it collapses to a smooth purée; the cut flesh browns quickly.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, straight from the tree; it does not keep

tree.notes: Described as hardy and at home on heavy soils; growers report large, regular crops of big, clean fruit even without spraying. Vigour, habit and bearing type are not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4 (group D) by Orange Pippin and the East of England Apples & Orchards Project. Self-fertility is not recorded, so plant a group 3-5 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist parts of Britain, including wet western hillsides and heavy-soiled eastern counties, where it crops reliably with little help.
climate.poor_climates: Not tried much in hot regions; early fruit with soft-textured, quickly bruised flesh is unlikely to hold up in hot summers.

health.other: Good scab resistance reported. Main drawbacks are fruit that bruises easily, browns quickly when cut and will not store.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a heavy or damp site in a cool region. Plan to use the crop quickly as sauce, juice or for eating fresh, and pair it with a mid-season flowering partner.

varieties.name: Hewes Crab

origin.parentage: Unknown; it is sometimes suggested to carry native American crab (Malus angustifolia) ancestry, but this is unproven

varieties.history: Virginia's classic colonial cider apple, described in the early nineteenth century from trees that were already said to be about a century old. It was planted at Monticello and on many Virginia plantations, and is now prized again by American craft cider makers.

look.description: Very small crab-like fruit, about 4 cm across, dull green streaked and overlaid with purplish dull red and peppered with pale dots.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, very juicy flesh that is sharply acidic with a noticeable astringent, slightly bitter edge. Too austere for most people raw; its value is a clear, dry, well-structured cider, on its own or in blends.
taste.best_eaten: Pressed Oct-Nov, after a short sweat

tree.notes: Long-lived, hardy tree that crops heavily but with a strong tendency to alternate years; thinning in the 'on' year helps even it out.

pollination.notes: Listed as group 3 and a good pollinator, with some self-fertility claimed; crops are better with a partner nearby.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer eastern US climates such as Virginia and the Mid-Atlantic, and also cold northern orchards where its hardiness counts.
climate.poor_climates: Few clear weaknesses recorded; in cool, cloudy summers the juice will be sharper and thinner.

health.other: Generally regarded as a tough, long-lived tree; main drawback is biennial bearing. Specific disease ratings are not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good backbone tree for a cider orchard in a cold or hot-summer area. Thin heavy crops to reduce alternate bearing, and blend its sharp, tannic juice with sweeter apples.

varieties.name: Hidden Rose
varieties.history: A chance seedling found in the 1960s on land belonging to Lucky and Audrey Newell near Airlie in Oregon's Willamette Valley. Louis Kimzey rediscovered the tree in the 1980s and it was commercialised under the trademark Hidden Rose, with Newell-Kimzey as the cultivar name.

look.description: Small, egg-shaped, plain yellow-green apple with prominent lenticels and at most a faint blush, hiding vivid pink-red flesh.

taste.summary: Very firm, crisp, juicy red flesh with a bright sweet-tart balance and fruity berry and citrus notes; quite sharp if picked early, sweeter after a few weeks, and it can last into February. Flavour depends on site: one grower found it never developed real flavour at a research station.

tree.notes: Fairly small tree with light, sometimes alternate crops; thin in spring to steady production.

pollination.notes: Reported as group 2; needs an early-flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates with long autumns, like western Oregon and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season northern sites may not ripen such a late apple; flesh colour may be weaker in hot climates.

health.other: Rated poor for general disease resistance, with some scab susceptibility.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs a long season and a warm, sheltered spot to ripen in Britain. Thin crops to avoid biennial bearing and plan for scab control in wet areas.

varieties.name: Hokuto

origin.place: Aomori Apple Experiment Station, Aomori, Japan
origin.parentage: Registered as Fuji x Mutsu, but later genetic work indicates the pollen parent was not Mutsu and is unidentified

varieties.history: Selected from a 1970 cross at the Aomori Apple Experiment Station, named in 1981 and registered in 1983. It was released as Fuji x Mutsu, but DNA studies since then point to a different pollen parent. Japanese tasters rate it among the best-flavoured apples, though it remains a niche variety.

look.description: Large, round to flattish apple, usually about 350 g and often over 600 g, deep purplish-red with stripes over a yellow ground.

taste.summary: Exceptionally juicy, firm cream flesh with a balanced sweet-sharp taste and a rich scent; fully ripe fruit often has watercore, giving glassy, honey-sweet patches.

tree.notes: Needs plenty of sun to colour. Listed as triploid by Pomiferous; given the doubt over its pollen parent, treat this as provisional.

pollination.notes: If triploid, a poor pollen donor: plant with two compatible diploids. UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Northern Japan's cool, sunny autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Little grown outside Japan; dull or short seasons are likely to leave this late apple under-coloured.

health.other: Prone to watercore and to mouldy core, which spoils the centre but not the surrounding flesh.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in the sunniest spot available with two diploid pollinators. Pick in late October or early November, store cold and eat by late winter, cutting out any mouldy core.

varieties.name: Holstein

origin.parentage: Seedling of Cox's Orange Pippin; pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: One of several Cox seedlings raised around 1918 by a teacher named Vahldik in Eutin, northern Germany (it was once known as his Cox seedling No. III). It became widely planted in northern Germany as a larger, easier relative of Cox.

look.description: Big, slightly conical apple, yellow with a broken orange flush and stripes and a light scattering of russet.

taste.summary: Juicy, fairly soft yet dense yellowish flesh, sweet with a richly spiced acidity when fully ripe and an aromatic, Cox-like character; several tasters note a pineapple flavour. Prized for its orange-tinted juice; keeps only a month or two and is best eaten cool.

tree.notes: A large, broad, vigorous triploid tree; use a dwarfing rootstock in gardens. Slow to come into bearing on stronger stocks.

pollination.notes: Triploid: a poor pollen donor, so plant two compatible diploids nearby (one to pollinate it and each other).

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist north-European climates such as northern Germany, Denmark and Britain, where it is less fussy than Cox.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to give soft, poorly flavoured fruit; little evidence of success in warm regions.

health.other: Generally healthier than Cox, with good scab resistance reported, but some susceptibility to canker, mildew and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: A good substitute for Cox where Cox sulks, especially in wetter northern gardens. Because it is triploid and vigorous, give it room or a dwarfing stock and make sure two diploid partners flower nearby.

varieties.name: Honeycrisp

origin.place: University of Minnesota Horticultural Research Center, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Keepsake x MN1627 (an unreleased selection with Duchess of Oldenburg and Golden Delicious as parents); originally recorded, wrongly, as Macoun x Honeygold
origin.raised_by: University of Minnesota apple breeding programme

varieties.history: Came from a 1960 cross in the University of Minnesota programme, tested as MN 1711 and released in 1991. DNA work later corrected its recorded parentage. Its exceptional crunch made it one of the most valuable apples in North America and the parent of many newer varieties.

look.description: Large, rounded apple, yellow mottled and striped with bright red, the amount of colour varying a lot with climate.

taste.summary: Famous for its texture: large cells that fracture with a light, juicy crunch rather than a hard, dense one. Flavour is mainly sweet with little acidity or depth, sometimes with a faint pear-drop or honeyed note; a well-grown fruit is refreshing, an ordinary one simply sweet. Stays crisp in store until spring, and the flavour can improve for a week or so after leaving cold storage.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Feb; crisp from the tree and still crisp after months in store

tree.notes: Weak-growing and easily stunted by early overcropping; thin hard and remove fruit in the first years. Prone to alternate bearing and to a zinc-related yellow blotching of leaves. Ripens unevenly, so pick over several passes and clip stalks short to avoid punctures.

pollination.notes: Needs a compatible diploid flowering at about the same time.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, cool-summer regions: Minnesota, Wisconsin, New England, eastern Canada, and similar northern Europe sites, where it colours well and keeps its texture.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give poor colour, softer fruit, sunburn and more storage disorders; quality from warm regions is noticeably lower.

health.other: Very prone to bitter pit, and to soft scald and soggy breakdown if put straight into cold storage (needs a week of conditioning at about 10 C). Leaf blotch/chlorosis and sunburn are common.

varieties.grow_notes: Best in a cold-winter, cool-summer climate on good, well-drained soil; it needs regular calcium sprays to limit bitter pit. Thin firmly every year and do not let a young tree crop heavily, or it stalls.

varieties.name: Honeygold

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Haralson

varieties.history: Crossed in 1935 at the University of Minnesota to give northern growers a Golden Delicious-type apple that survives their winters, and released around 1970 (the university's own listing gives 1966). It is often wrongly cited as a parent of Honeycrisp.

look.description: Golden-yellow to yellow-green apple, sometimes with a faint bronze-red cheek; looks much like Golden Delicious.

taste.summary: Close to Golden Delicious but sweeter and milder, with crisp, juicy cream flesh and a honeyed sweetness. The low acidity strikes some tasters as bland, while others find enough balance to enjoy it.

tree.notes: Hardy, productive tree; little else distinctive is recorded about its growth.

pollination.notes: Group 3 (Orange Pippin). Needs a diploid partner; Haralson or a hardy crab works in cold regions.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern gardens (roughly zones 4 and sheltered 3) that are too harsh for Golden Delicious itself.
climate.poor_climates: Hot climates, where Golden Delicious grows anyway and Honeygold offers no advantage; fruit can be soft and dull after warm autumns.

health.other: Rated susceptible to fire blight by the University of Minnesota; other disease behaviour is poorly recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on a sunny, well-drained site and avoid heavy nitrogen, which encourages soft, blight-prone growth. Cut out any fire blight strikes well below the visible damage.

varieties.name: Howgate Wonder

origin.place: Howgate Lane, Bembridge, Isle of Wight, England
origin.parentage: Blenheim Orange x Newton Wonder

varieties.history: Raised on the Isle of Wight in 1915-16 by crossing Blenheim Orange with Newton Wonder, it won an RHS Award of Merit in 1929 and was introduced by Stuart Low & Co. in 1932. Famous for the sheer size of its fruit and holds a current RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Very large, broad, flat-sided apple, yellow with streaks and a flush of orange-red.

taste.summary: Firm, fine, juicy cream flesh, only moderately sharp and quite sweet once ripe, with a faint aroma. Cooks to a light-flavoured puree that keeps some texture; by midwinter it is pleasant raw, though plainer than a true dessert apple.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar; sweeter for eating raw after Christmas

tree.notes: A vigorous, spreading tree that crops heavily; thin fruitlets to get the largest apples and support heavy-laden branches.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly late (group 4 in most lists, 3 in some); partly self-fertile like its parent Newton Wonder but crops better with a partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist temperate climates across Britain, including the north and west; rated hardy to about -20 C.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, dry summers are likely to reduce size and colour; not known from warm-climate orchards.

health.other: Generally healthy and well suited to organic growing; resists bitter pit in store.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it room or a dwarfing rootstock, as it is vigorous. A reliable, heavy-cropping alternative to Bramley that also yields fruit you can eat raw late in the winter.

varieties.name: Hubbardston Nonesuch
varieties.history: Found in the town of Hubbardston in central Massachusetts in the early 1800s and recorded by the early 1830s. It was a respected New England market and home-orchard apple through the nineteenth century, though it never caught on widely in the South.

look.description: Large, rather lopsided fruit with a yellow base heavily washed and streaked with dull to bright red; colour varies a lot with site.

taste.summary: Tender to moderately firm, juicy white flesh that is distinctly sweet with only gentle acidity and a full, rounded apple flavour. It keeps its texture well for a month or two and the flavour deepens somewhat in store.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing, reported to come into bearing early and to crop regularly; responds to standard winter spur pruning.

pollination.notes: Listed as a mid-late (group 4) diploid; plant with another group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool to warm temperate regions with cold winters, such as New England, New York and the upper Midwest.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid lowlands give poorly coloured, soft fruit; very short seasons may not ripen it fully.

health.other: Reported to have good scab resistance but some susceptibility to canker.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a cold-winter garden that wants a sweet, large dessert apple. Give it full sun for the best colour and a pollinator in a similar flowering group.

varieties.name: Hyslop
varieties.history: An old crab of unknown origin grown in North America since at least the nineteenth century and painted for the USDA pomological watercolour collection. It is valued for its striking dark fruit and for jelly and cider.

look.description: Large for a crab, over 5 cm, deep red to purplish-red under a heavy blue-grey bloom.

taste.summary: Firm yellow flesh, juicy at first but soon mealy, with a mildly acid and distinctly astringent flavour. Used for jelly, pickling and cider blends rather than eating raw.
taste.best_eaten: Soon after picking, for jelly or pickling

tree.notes: Tree habit not documented in the sources consulted.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded in the sources consulted.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern North American climates, where it was historically grown.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Disease profile not documented in the sources consulted; ripe fruit becomes mealy quickly.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage crab for cold gardens, worth growing for its dark, bloomy fruit and as a tannic jelly or cider crab. Process the fruit promptly after picking.

varieties.name: Idared

origin.place: Idaho Agricultural Experiment Station, Moscow, Idaho
origin.parentage: Jonathan x Wagener

varieties.history: Bred by Leif Verner at the Idaho station in the 1930s and introduced in 1942. Its heavy crops and very long storage life made it a major commercial apple in Europe, especially Poland, for decades.

look.description: Flattish, glossy apple almost covered in bright red over a pale green-yellow ground, with smooth clean skin.

taste.summary: Crisp, fine white flesh, juicy but rather plain when first picked; after a few months in store it becomes sweeter with a light vinous tang. Holds its shape when baked or cooked.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Apr; improves after a couple of months in store

tree.notes: Comes into bearing quickly and crops heavily; thin to keep size and colour. Early blossom can be caught by frost.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; pair it with a group 1-3 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Continental climates with cold winters and warm summers: central and eastern Europe, the US Midwest and Northeast.
climate.poor_climates: Frost pockets (early blossom), and humid warm areas where mildew and fire blight run rampant.

health.other: Very susceptible to powdery mildew and fire blight; early flowering makes it vulnerable to spring frost.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant away from frost pockets and keep mildew in check by removing infected shoot tips in spring. A good dual-purpose keeper for anyone with cool storage space.

varieties.name: Ingrid Marie

origin.parentage: Chance seedling; a 2011 DNA study gives Cox's Orange Pippin x Cox's Pomona

varieties.history: A chance seedling found around 1910 in the grounds of a school on Funen and named after the finder's daughter, who died young. Sold in Denmark from 1936 and Sweden from 1946, it became a mainstay of Scandinavian orchards and a parent of Elstar and the Swedish Aroma.

look.description: Round to slightly flattened apple, marbled dark red over most of a yellow-green skin, sprinkled with pale brown lenticels; red often stains the flesh just under the skin.

taste.summary: Tender, juicy, yellowish-white flesh with a fresh sweet-tart balance; Scandinavian sources praise its pleasant aroma and one taster finds a hint of Cox, but Orange Pippin rates the flavour light and rather bland. Best soon after picking, though it can be stored into the new year; a traditional Christmas apple in Scandinavia.

tree.notes: Grows well in moderately warm, humid climates; avoid poorly drained ground where canker takes hold.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering, assigned to UK group 3 approximately; pollinated by Cox-season diploids.

climate.best_climates: Mild maritime Scandinavia (Denmark, southern Sweden) and similar cool, humid climates such as the UK.
climate.poor_climates: Cold inland areas beyond southern Swedish zones; hot summers are likely to spoil colour and texture.

health.other: Fruit-tree canker is the main weakness, especially on heavy, wet soils.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose a well-drained site and cut out canker promptly. Pair with another mid-season diploid such as Cox or James Grieve.

varieties.name: Irish Peach
varieties.history: An old Irish apple, probably from County Sligo, that reached English nurseries around 1820. Victorian gardeners rated it one of the best-flavoured very early apples, and it has been widely grown across Europe under many translated names.

look.description: Smallish to medium, slightly ribbed round-conical apple, green-yellow with a dull orange-red flush and streaks on the sunny side.

taste.summary: White, very juicy flesh that is soft rather than crisp, with a lively, rather sharp flavour and a distinct peach-like aroma that gives the variety its name. It does not keep: eat within days of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Early-mid Aug, straight from the tree

tree.notes: A tip-bearer with a spreading, flat-topped habit; unsuitable for cordons or espaliers. Prune lightly, renewing old wood rather than shortening every shoot. Fruit drops when ripe.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2); needs another early or early-mid season diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist maritime climates such as Ireland, western Britain and Scandinavia, where it ripens slowly enough to keep its flavour.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers make the fruit ripen and soften almost overnight; early blossom is vulnerable in frost pockets.

health.other: Generally healthy. Weaknesses are practical: tip-bearing habit, fruit drop and virtually no keeping life.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for wetter western and northern gardens. Grow as a bush or half-standard rather than a trained form, and visit the tree daily in August as the fruit ripens.

varieties.name: James Grieve

origin.parentage: Seedling of Pott's Seedling or Cox's Orange Pippin; pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: Raised in Edinburgh by James Grieve and introduced by his employers, the Dicksons nursery, being first recorded in 1893; it won an RHS Award of Merit in 1897 and a First Class Certificate in 1906. It became a favourite in northern Europe and is a parent of Katy, Lord Lambourne, Greensleeves and Elton Beauty.

look.description: Pale yellow apple flushed and broken-striped with red, with a faint satiny sheen.

taste.summary: Exceptionally juicy, soft, open-textured flesh with a bright, tangy acidity when first picked, good for cooking as well as eating. After a week or two it mellows to a sweeter, gentler apple.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct; sharp and good for cooking when first picked, sweeter after a couple of weeks

tree.notes: Compact-to-moderate spur-bearer that crops early and regularly; adapts well to trained forms. The fruit bruises at a touch and may drop when ripe, so pick carefully over several passes.

pollination.notes: Partly self-fertile and an excellent pollinator for other group 2-4 diploids.

climate.best_climates: Cool, short-summer climates: Scotland, northern England, Germany and Scandinavia, where it crops reliably and keeps its zesty acidity.
climate.poor_climates: Warm wet lowlands encourage canker, and hot summers give soft, quickly-mealy fruit with poor colour.

health.other: Prone to canker on wet, heavy or poorly drained soils; some scab in damp seasons. The fruit bruises very easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable choice for colder and northern gardens and a useful pollinator. Plant on free-draining soil to limit canker, cut out cankered wood promptly, and pick early for cooking or later for dessert.

varieties.name: Jazz

origin.place: Havelock North, Hawke's Bay, New Zealand
origin.parentage: Royal Gala x Braeburn
origin.raised_by: HortResearch (now Plant & Food Research), with ENZA

varieties.history: Bred in Hawke's Bay by the New Zealand government research institute now called Plant & Food Research, from a 1985 Royal Gala x Braeburn cross, and launched commercially in the early 2000s. Jazz is the trademark; the cultivar name is Scifresh, and it is grown only under licence in both hemispheres, including in Kent.

look.description: Medium, slightly conical fruit flushed red to maroon over green-yellow and orange, with fine pale lenticels.

taste.summary: A very hard, dense, crunchy apple with juicy butter-yellow flesh and a strong sweet-sharp flavour led by a pronounced pear-drop note; tasters also report floral, honeyed and occasionally banana or clove hints. Well-coloured fruit tastes best - poorly coloured apples are flatter and closer to Braeburn - and the firmness holds for months in store.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar; keeps its crunch well in store

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing. A licensed club variety: trees are generally only available to contracted commercial growers, so garden plantings are rare. Needs good light into the canopy for colour.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 3; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Sunny regions with a long growing season and cool autumn nights, such as Hawke's Bay, Washington, the Western Cape, north Italy and the warmer fruit areas of southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons leave it under-ripe and poorly coloured, which costs it most of its flavour; very hot autumns also limit colour.

health.other: Disease ratings are not well published; both parents (Gala and Braeburn) are prone to European canker and fire blight, and Braeburn to bitter pit, so treat Jazz as at risk of these.

varieties.grow_notes: Only practical where the season is long enough for a late-October harvest with good colour. Grow in full sun with open pruning so light reaches the fruit, and thin early. Pollinate with a group 2-4 diploid.

varieties.name: Jelly King
varieties.history: A New Zealand crab of the late twentieth century, registered as 'Mattfru' and sold as Jelly King. As the name says, it was selected for jelly-making, with unusually large fruit for a crab, and it holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Large for a crab apple; yellow flushed orange-pink to red, and the fruit persists on the tree after ripening.

taste.summary: Sharp and juicy, rated very good for the kitchen; it makes a well-coloured, well-set jelly and the large fruit is quicker to prepare than tiny crabs.

tree.notes: Vigorous, upright tree that crops heavily; suitable for organic growing and beginners.

pollination.notes: Pale pink buds opening to white blossom; a good pollinator for mid-season apples.

climate.best_climates: Cool to warm temperate climates such as the UK and New Zealand.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; rated hardy to about -20 C, so very severe winters may be a limit.

health.other: Rated good overall disease resistance by nursery sources.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in sun on any well-drained soil and give it room, as it is more vigorous than most garden crabs. Pick in late September for jelly; a useful mid-season pollinator.

varieties.name: Jester

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Worcester Pearmain x Starkspur Golden Delicious
origin.raised_by: Dr F.H. Alston, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Raised by Frank Alston at East Malling in 1966 and released in 1981 as a well-coloured, heavy-cropping modern garden apple. It never became a major commercial variety.

look.description: Smooth, attractive apple with a creamy-yellow ground, flushed and streaked bright red; skin becomes greasy in store.

taste.summary: Crisp to softish, very juicy white flesh with a sweet, light flavour and little sharpness. Pleasant and refreshing rather than complex, and popular with children.

tree.notes: Regular, heavy and early cropper of average vigour; straightforward to prune as a spur-bearer.

pollination.notes: Fairly late flowering, which helps it avoid frost; plant with a group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp temperate climates like southern England, where it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Little grown outside Britain; hot summers likely give soft fruit and poorer colour.

health.other: Reported as having average all-round disease resistance; good blossom frost tolerance.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, reliable garden apple for southern Britain, good for a family wanting sweet, colourful fruit. Grow on a dwarfing rootstock as a bush or cordon and thin in heavy years.

varieties.name: John Downie
varieties.history: Raised in the 1870s by the Lichfield nurseryman Edward Holmes and named after his fellow nurseryman John Downie. It has long been considered the finest British crab for jelly and is one of the few crabs worth eating raw.

look.description: A comparatively large crab, roughly 3 cm, shaped like an upturned pear; yellow to orange with a bright scarlet flush on the sunny side and a glossy finish.

taste.summary: Sharp, tangy and juicy with more real apple flavour than most crabs, so acid-lovers can eat it straight from the tree. Its fame rests on jelly, which is richly flavoured and a pretty amber-pink to orange-red.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, for jelly; raw once fully coloured

tree.notes: Narrow and upright when young, broadening later, so it fits smaller gardens than most crabs (3-5 m after ten years on a semi-vigorous stock). Fruit does not hang as long as the persistent ornamental crabs.

pollination.notes: Generous white blossom from pink buds; a popular pollinator for mid-season apples. UK sources list it in group 3 or 4.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens in Britain and northern Europe on fertile, well-drained soil with good air movement.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid areas where scab can disfigure and partly defoliate it; humid summer heat brings fire blight risk.

health.other: Rather prone to apple scab, which can mark the fruit and drop leaves early in wet years, though the crop is still fine for jelly. Formerly held the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

varieties.grow_notes: Site it in sun with free air circulation and clear fallen leaves in autumn to reduce scab. Pick for jelly as soon as the fruit colours, before it drops, and use it as a pollinator for mid-season dessert apples.

varieties.name: Jonagold

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Jonathan
origin.raised_by: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station (Cornell University)

varieties.history: Raised from a 1943 cross at the Geneva station and released in 1968. It became hugely popular with European growers, especially in Belgium and the Netherlands, and has produced dozens of redder sports such as Jonagored.

look.description: Large, rounded golden-yellow apple, flushed and striped orange-red over about half the surface.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, creamy-white flesh with a honeyed sweetness from Golden Delicious, kept lively by plenty of balancing acidity from Jonathan; some tasters note a subtle pear-drop sweetness. Best within a month or two of picking: it softens quickly out of the fridge and turns greasy in long storage, so supermarket fruit is often disappointing.

tree.notes: Vigorous triploid that crops well and early; thin to avoid overcropping and small fruit.

pollination.notes: Triploid, so a poor pollen donor; needs two diploid partners nearby. Sources advise against relying on Golden Delicious (a parent) as its pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool-summer climates: Belgium, the Netherlands, northern Germany, Pacific Northwest coast, Michigan and New York.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give soft fruit with poor colour and sunburn, which is why it lost ground in warmer US regions.
