varieties.grow_notes: Use sparingly in blends for sugar and tannin. Plant with other very late bloomers such as Dabinett or Stoke Red. Its late blossom avoids most spring frosts.

varieties.name: Melba

origin.place: Central Experimental Farm, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
origin.parentage: McIntosh seedling; the pollen parent is often given as Liveland Raspberry but is not firmly documented
origin.raised_by: W. T. Macoun, Central Experimental Farm

varieties.history: Raised in 1898 by W. T. Macoun at Canada's Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa and released in 1909; it is generally said to be named after the opera singer Nellie Melba. It won the American Pomological Society's Wilder Medal in 1927 and became a leading summer apple in Canada and Scandinavia.

look.description: Pale yellow apple washed and striped with pinkish to crimson red, with a whitish bloom and somewhat ribbed shape.

taste.summary: Snow-white, crisp and juicy flesh that softens fairly quickly, with a sweet, lightly tart, wine-like flavour and the perfumed skin aroma typical of the McIntosh family. Also makes good sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-early Sep; eat soon after picking or use for sauce

tree.notes: Very productive and bears young, but strongly inclined to alternate cropping; thin hard in heavy years. Fruit bruises easily.

pollination.notes: UK flowering group not reliably published; National Fruit Collection blossom dates are early-to-mid season, similar to Beauty of Bath.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental and northern climates such as eastern Canada, the northern US and Scandinavia, where it is very winter-hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Hot humid summers bring soft fruit, poor colour and heavy scab pressure; mild, wet maritime climates also favour scab.

health.other: Susceptible to scab like other McIntosh offspring; strongly biennial; fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the hardiest good-quality summer apples, worth growing in cold districts. Thin fruit every year to curb biennial bearing, and spray or choose an open, airy site where scab is common.

varieties.name: Melrose

origin.place: Ohio Agricultural Experiment Station, Wooster, Ohio
origin.parentage: Jonathan x Red Delicious
origin.raised_by: Freeman S. Howlett, Ohio Agricultural Experiment Station

varieties.history: Bred by Freeman Howlett at Wooster from a cross made in the 1930s and introduced in 1944; it is the official state apple of Ohio. It found a second home in Europe, where it became a significant late-keeping variety in Belgium, northern France and Poland.

look.description: Broad, flattish fruit streaked and flushed dark red over yellow-green, with patches of russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse but juicy cream flesh with a Jonathan-like sweet-sharp balance, milder than Jonathan; some tasters notice pineapple. Plain when first picked and then best in pies, it develops a fuller, fruity aroma after two or three months in store, from around Christmas.

tree.notes: Vigorous, vase-shaped tree that crops heavily and regularly; scab control is usually needed.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; average pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental and north-west European climates (Ohio, Belgium, Poland) with cool autumns that colour the fruit and a long enough season to finish it.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid areas without a spray programme because of scab; warm-night regions give poorer colour.

health.other: Scab is the main problem; slightly prone to mildew; some resistance to cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it space or a semi-dwarfing rootstock and an open, airy site to limit scab. Pick in mid October and store for several weeks before eating.

varieties.name: Mère de Ménage
varieties.history: Known in Britain by the late 1700s, but its origin is uncertain. Bunyard considered it most probably Continental (it was grown in Belgium as Queen Emma) but distinct from the French apple of the same name. It was widely grown in East Anglia as a long-keeping kitchen apple. Old catalogues often confuse it with Gloria Mundi and other giant cookers.

look.description: Very large, irregular, ribbed, flat-conical fruit; almost covered with dull brownish-crimson and broad darker stripes, scattered with conspicuous pale dots.

taste.summary: Firm, coarse, greenish flesh with a brisk, sharp flavour, juicy when fresh but drier in store. A first-rate cooker in its day and a good keeper.

tree.notes: Bunyard describes a vigorous tree that grows large and spreading, with only moderate cropping. Give it room.

pollination.notes: No published group found. Estimated as group 3 from National Fruit Collection flowering dates. Ploidy is unrecorded, so plant two partners to be safe.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate lowlands of eastern England and the Low Countries, where it was traditionally grown.
climate.poor_climates: No record from warm climates. A late, large apple that probably needs a long, mild autumn.

health.other: Disease responses are not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage curiosity for a large garden or orchard. Plant it on a vigorous rootstock with plenty of space, and store the fruit cool for winter cooking.

varieties.name: Meridian

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Maidstone, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Falstaff x Cox's Orange Pippin
origin.raised_by: Dr Frank Alston, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Bred at East Malling by Frank Alston from Falstaff and Cox and introduced in 1999 as a Cox-flavoured apple that is easier to grow. It has been sold mainly to gardeners rather than commercial growers.

look.description: Clean, smooth apple with a green-yellow ground, flushed and striped orange-red, with little russet.

taste.summary: Crisp and exceptionally juicy, with a delicate, well-balanced sweet-sharp flavour in the Cox mould but with less depth; tasters pick out hints of lemon and melon. Best within two or three weeks of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Nov, within a few weeks of picking

tree.notes: Average vigour, regular and heavy cropping spur-bearer; thin in heavy years.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Cool, temperate English-type climates; bred for gardens in southern Britain.
climate.poor_climates: Little grown outside Britain; hot summers are likely to soften fruit and dull colour.

health.other: Good general disease resistance with some resistance to scab and mildew; some susceptibility to woolly aphid.

varieties.grow_notes: A low-fuss alternative to Cox for gardens in southern and central Britain. Plant with any mid-season pollinator and eat the fruit fairly soon after picking, as it does not keep long.

varieties.name: Merton Russet

origin.place: John Innes Horticultural Institution, Merton, Surrey (now south London), England
origin.parentage: Sturmer Pippin x Cox's Orange Pippin
origin.raised_by: M.B. Crane, John Innes Horticultural Institution

varieties.history: A deliberate cross made in 1921 by M.B. Crane at the John Innes institute in Merton, combining the long-keeping Sturmer Pippin with Cox. It was named in 1943 and is kept in the National Fruit Collection, but it never became a commercial apple.

look.description: Medium, truncated-conical fruit with a yellow ground largely overlaid by russet, showing some red flush through it.

taste.summary: Small golden russet from a Sturmer Pippin x Cox cross, with very crisp, juicy, deep-yellow flesh and a complex sweet, spicy flavour. A late apple that holds its quality into the winter.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Feb, after some weeks in store

tree.notes: Little published growing data. Both parents are diploid spur-bearers, so treat it as a normal spur-pruned diploid until it shows otherwise.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 2 and flowers early at Brogdale; pair with an early-to-mid flowering diploid (groups 1-3).

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate lowland Britain and similar maritime climates with long, mild autumns to finish a mid-October apple.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or very cold climates; very short seasons may not ripen it, and hot summers are likely to blunt its acidity.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded. Its Cox parent passes on canker and mildew susceptibility to many offspring, so watch for both.

varieties.grow_notes: A collector's russet for a sunny, sheltered garden in southern Britain. Plant with an early-flowering partner, pick in mid October and store cool to eat after Christmas.

varieties.name: Michaelmas Red

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: McIntosh x Worcester Pearmain
origin.raised_by: H. M. Tydeman, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: Raised in 1929 by H. M. Tydeman at East Malling from McIntosh x Worcester Pearmain, the same cross that produced Tydeman's Early Worcester. The National Fruit Collection lists it as Tydeman's Michaelmas Red; the name refers to ripening around Michaelmas (29 September).

look.description: Medium, truncate-conical fruit with greenish-yellow skin largely covered by streaked red.

taste.summary: Rather soft, very juicy greenish-white flesh with a sweet, refreshing, vinous flavour that shows its McIntosh parentage.

tree.notes: Little growing information is recorded; it is rarely planted outside collections. Both parents are diploid.

pollination.notes: No published group found. Estimated as group 3 from National Fruit Collection flowering dates; plant a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate climates like south-east England. Its McIntosh and Worcester parents both colour best with cool autumn nights.
climate.poor_climates: Warm-night regions are likely to give poorly coloured, soft fruit (inferred from its parents).

health.other: Disease behaviour is not recorded for this variety.

varieties.grow_notes: A collector's early-autumn dessert apple. Grow it like Tydeman's Early Worcester in a sunny, open spot, and eat the fruit fresh because the soft flesh does not keep long.

varieties.name: Michelin

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: Raised by the Yvetot nurseryman Legrand, it first fruited in 1872 and was named after the cider pomologist Henri Michelin. Herefordshire's Woolhope Club brought it to England in the 1880s, and despite being scarce in France it became one of the most planted English cider apples of the twentieth century.

look.description: Small-to-medium green apple, similar to Brown Snout but without the russet patch at the eye.

taste.summary: A medium bittersweet with good sugar, low acid and fair tannin; reliable but rather neutral, so it is usually blended rather than used alone.

tree.notes: Valued for dependable, regular heavy crops without strong biennialism; a long-standing commercial partner for Dabinett.

pollination.notes: Partly self-fertile; often used as a pollinator in bush cider orchards.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist maritime climates; widely grown in English and New World cider orchards.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season areas; humid regions with heavy scab pressure.

health.other: Scab reports vary from some resistance to moderate susceptibility.

varieties.grow_notes: A reliable workhorse cider apple for blending. Grows well in intensive bush orchards. Pick when fruit starts to drop.

varieties.name: Miller's Seedling
varieties.history: Raised in 1848 by James Miller at Newbury in Berkshire and given an RHS Award of Merit in 1906. Popular with Victorian and Edwardian gardeners as a sweet, juicy early apple; a redder sport, Red Miller, also exists.

look.description: Pale greenish-yellow, flattish apple with a light pink-red flush and fine red stripes on the sunny side.

taste.summary: White, very juicy flesh, crisp but light when first picked and soon softening, with a sweet, refreshingly tart and fragrant flavour. It bruises at the slightest knock and goes waxy within about a week, so eat it straight from the tree.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-mid Sep, fresh from the tree

tree.notes: Crops very heavily in its 'on' years and then rests, so thin fruitlets hard to even out cropping.

pollination.notes: Usually placed in early flowering group 2 (one guide gives 3); partly self-fertile but sets better with a partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild temperate climates like southern and central England.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers make the soft, easily bruised fruit deteriorate even faster; no records from hot regions.

health.other: Average disease resistance. Main faults are a strong biennial habit and fruit that bruises very easily.

varieties.grow_notes: A rewarding sweet early apple for gardens if thinned every year to avoid feast-and-famine cropping. Handle the fruit gently and eat or juice it within a week of picking.

varieties.name: Mollie's Delicious

origin.place: New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, New Brunswick, New Jersey
origin.parentage: (Golden Delicious x Edgewood) x (Red Gravenstein x Close); not a sport of Red Delicious despite the name
origin.raised_by: G.W. Schneider, New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station (Rutgers)

varieties.history: Crossed in 1948 in the Rutgers apple programme in New Jersey and released in 1966. Despite its name it has no connection with Red Delicious; Golden Delicious and Gravenstein sit in its pedigree, and it was later used as a parent in the PRI scab-resistance programme that produced Williams' Pride.

look.description: Big, tall, strongly ribbed fruit with a yellow skin washed and mottled with pinkish to bright red.

taste.summary: Sweet and mild, reminiscent of a fresher, slightly sharper Golden Delicious, with cream flesh that is juicy and fairly crisp when picked at the right moment but can turn soft and starchy if picked early or left too long. Noted for a pleasant lingering aftertaste.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, fresh from the tree; keeps better than most earlies in a fridge

tree.notes: Little UK growing data. In the southern USA it has a reputation as one of the few good apples that fruits reliably in mild-winter areas.

pollination.notes: Sources differ: Brogdale records it flowering a few days after Cox, while Orange Pippin lists group 5. Plant with a group 3-5 diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Warm-temperate areas with hot summers and fairly mild winters, such as the US mid-Atlantic and upper South, where it ripens well ahead of the worst heat.
climate.poor_climates: Colour is slow to develop where nights stay warm, so fruit may stay mostly green in the Deep South; in cool, dull summers the fruit may lack sweetness. Chill figure is an estimate from its reported success in mild-winter regions.

health.other: Rated very resistant to cedar-apple rust by the University of Arkansas. Other disease behaviour poorly recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good early apple for warmer gardens where Cox-types struggle. Give it full sun to help the blush develop and a mid-to-late flowering partner; pick when the ground colour turns from green to yellow.

varieties.name: Monidel

origin.parentage: Red-coloured bud sport of Delbarestivale (Delcorf)

varieties.history: A redder-skinned bud sport of Delbarestivale (Delcorf), the early French dessert apple raised at the Delbard nurseries. It is treated as the same apple as its parent apart from the stronger red colour.

look.description: Yellow apple heavily striped and flushed red, redder overall than ordinary Delbarestivale.

taste.summary: As Delbarestivale: sweet, juicy and fairly crisp, with a gentle aromatic quality and low sharpness. Best eaten soon after picking.

tree.notes: Growth should match Delbarestivale; no independent data found for the sport itself.

pollination.notes: Needs a pollinator. Group inferred from Brogdale flowering records for the parent Delcorf, which blooms with James Grieve.

climate.best_climates: Western European climates from southern England to France, where the parent variety is grown commercially for the early market.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in very cold or very hot regions; values are inferred from the parent variety and French origin.

health.other: No disease data found for the sport; expect it to behave like Delbarestivale.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow as you would Delbarestivale in a sunny, sheltered spot. The extra red colour is the reason to choose it; provide a group 2-4 partner.

varieties.name: Muscadet de Dieppe
varieties.history: An old Normandy cider apple named after the Channel port of Dieppe and recorded from around the mid-eighteenth century. It is one of the earliest French cider apples to ripen and is held in the UK National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Small, broadly conical fruit, green to yellow with a dark red to orange-red striped and mottled flush; firm cream flesh.

taste.summary: A mild bittersweet with sweet, aromatic juice: low acid and moderate tannin, softer and more fragrant than the heavy Norman bitters. Useful for early-season cider.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill Sep-Oct within a couple of weeks of picking

tree.notes: Ploidy is reported inconsistently (listed as triploid in some cider tables, diploid in others). Crops reasonably.

pollination.notes: Very early flowering, among the first cider apples in blossom; partners must also flower early.

climate.best_climates: Maritime climates with few late spring frosts, such as coastal Normandy and southern England.
climate.poor_climates: Frost pockets and continental areas with late spring frosts, which catch its very early blossom.

health.other: Early blossom is the main risk (spring frost). Reported to have some resistance to fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on a frost-free slope rather than in a hollow. Because it ripens early, press it separately or with other September apples rather than holding it for the main late harvest.

varieties.name: Nehou

origin.place: France (probably Normandy; the name matches the village of Néhou in the Cotentin)

varieties.history: A French bittersweet brought to England in the 1920s by Dr H.E. Durham for the Hereford cider makers H.P. Bulmer. It is valued for very high tannin and an excellent, fruity, full-bodied cider.

look.description: Small to medium, oblong-conical yellow fruit with only a faint washed orange flush; soft and easily bruised.

taste.summary: A full bittersweet with very high tannin and little acid, giving a heavy, astringent but fruity juice; cider made from it is rich and full-bodied. The flesh is soft.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill Oct, handle gently as it bruises

tree.notes: Average vigour and very quick to crop, but the NFC records it as a biennial cropper.

pollination.notes: Fairly early flowering over a long period; a good pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild maritime cider regions such as Herefordshire, Somerset and Normandy.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid sites where scab is severe; hot climates untested.

health.other: Susceptible to scab; soft fruit bruises easily; biennial bearing.

varieties.grow_notes: Spray or site it carefully against scab, and thin in heavy years to even out cropping. Use small amounts in blends to add tannin and body.

varieties.name: Newton Wonder

origin.parentage: Probably Dumelow's Seedling x Blenheim Orange

varieties.history: Found by a Mr Taylor at King's Newton in Derbyshire (traditionally growing at the village inn) and released around 1887, when it also earned an RHS First Class Certificate. Its likely parents are Dumelow's Seedling and Blenheim Orange; it in turn fathered Howgate Wonder.

look.description: Large, flattish fruit, bright yellow with a scarlet flush and stripes over the sunny half.

taste.summary: A large cooker with sharp, acidic flesh that is crisp and very juicy at picking, though a little sweeter than Bramley; it cooks to a puree needing little sugar. After a few months in store, by about Christmas, it softens and mellows into a pleasant sweet-sharp eating apple.

tree.notes: Very vigorous and wide-spreading; slow to start but then crops heavily, with a strong tendency to biennial bearing. Thin in heavy years.

pollination.notes: Late flowering (group 4 in some lists, 5 in others); partly self-fertile but better with a late-flowering partner. Blossom has good frost tolerance.

climate.best_climates: Cool, damp temperate climates throughout Britain; its late blossom helps it avoid spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to cut storage life and colour; untested in warm regions.

health.other: Some resistance to scab and canker; somewhat susceptible to powdery mildew. Biennial cropping is the main practical nuisance.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs space or a dwarfing rootstock because of its vigour. A good late-flowering cooker for frosty sites; thin hard in heavy years to even out cropping.

varieties.name: Newtown Pippin

origin.place: Newtown (now Elmhurst), Queens, Long Island, New York

varieties.history: A chance seedling from Newtown on Long Island in the early 1700s, and one of the first American apples exported to Britain; it was later grown in Virginia as Albemarle Pippin and admired by Jefferson. In the 20th century it became a processing and juice apple in California and Oregon.

look.description: Somewhat lopsided, flattened apple, grass-green ripening to yellowish-green, sometimes with a faint pinkish cheek and russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Hard, tight-grained and rather unappetising straight off the tree; after one to two months in store it turns crisp and juicy with a tart-sweet, wine-like and richly aromatic flavour, famously said to carry a hint of pineapple. The cut flesh browns quickly. A versatile apple for eating, pies, juice and cider.

tree.notes: Slow to start cropping and inclined to biennial bearing; needs fertile soil and a long season to finish its fruit.

pollination.notes: Diploid; plant with another variety flowering in groups 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm growing seasons: the Virginia Piedmont, coastal California (Watsonville) and Oregon's Hood River valley.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short summers such as Britain's and New England's leave it small, green and sour.

health.other: Moderate susceptibility to most diseases; prone to storage disorders including bitter pit and internal browning.

varieties.grow_notes: Only worth growing where autumns are long and warm. Give rich, well-drained soil and a pollinator, thin heavy crops to limit biennial bearing, and store before eating.

varieties.name: Nonpareil
varieties.history: A very old russet apple, generally believed to be French, that reached England around the mid-16th century. It was one of the most esteemed dessert apples of the 17th to 19th centuries and gave its name to a whole group of 'Nonpareil' russets.

look.description: Small to medium, flattish fruit, greenish yellow under a heavy coat of russet dots and patches, sometimes with a faint brownish-red flush.

taste.summary: One of the small group of pear-drop apples: a strong pear-drop flavour with lively, wine-like acidity and an aftertaste some growers liken to honey and pear. Growers disagree on texture, some finding the flesh soft and sponge-like with modest juice, others surprisingly juicy. Best kept until mid-winter, when it sweetens.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous spur-bearer; little modern detail on habit or regularity.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not reliably published; at Brogdale it flowers in the early-to-mid part of the season, so a group 2-3 partner is a safe choice.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites in southern England and northern France, where it has a long autumn to build sugar before picking.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, wet northern sites where a late apple may not ripen; very hot summers are likely to cost it the sharpness that defines it.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded in modern trials.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it the warmest wall or sheltered sunny spot available, as old growers did. Pick in mid October and store cool; the flavour is not at its best until mid-winter.

varieties.name: Norfolk Beauty

origin.place: Gunton Park, near Norwich, Norfolk, England
origin.parentage: Warner's King x Waltham Abbey Seedling
origin.raised_by: Mr Allan, gardener at Gunton Park

varieties.history: Raised by Allan, head gardener at Gunton Park in Norfolk, from a cross of Warner's King with Waltham Abbey Seedling. It was introduced in 1902, the year it received both an Award of Merit and a First Class Certificate from the RHS.

look.description: Large, flattened-round fruit with pale lemon to whitish-yellow skin, a faint red flush and a little russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Rather soft, loose, somewhat dry flesh with a clean acidity. It cooks quickly to a creamy froth that needs little sugar and has a light lemony note.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous to fairly large. Bunyard said it crops well only once the tree is established, so expect a slow start.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 8 May, so group 2 is inferred. Needs an early-to-mid season partner.

climate.best_climates: Eastern England and similar cool, fairly dry lowland climates.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance in hot or very cold climates; values are inferred from its English origin.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good autumn cooker for East Anglian gardens, giving large fruit that need little sugar. Give the young tree a few years to establish before expecting full crops.

varieties.name: Norfolk Beefing
varieties.history: An old Norfolk apple: estate records from 1698 mention it being sent to London for Robert Walpole, though the National Fruit Collection's first formal record is 1807. It was famous for 'biffins', whole apples slowly baked and pressed flat, which Norwich bakers sold and Dickens mentions in A Christmas Carol.

look.description: Large, flattish and somewhat ribbed, green-yellow under an extensive dull crimson to maroon flush and streaks, darkening in store.

taste.summary: Very firm, coarse, juicy flesh that is strongly acidic at picking. It sweetens slowly in store and by late winter or spring can be eaten fresh; baked or dried it becomes dense, rich and sweet.
taste.best_eaten: Cook from Jan; raw by Mar-Jun once mellowed

tree.notes: Vigorous and a heavy, regular cropper; thin fruitlets in heavy years. Sources disagree on ploidy (one lists it as triploid, another as diploid), so do not rely on it as a pollinator.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not reliably published; it flowers mid-season at Brogdale. Ploidy is disputed, so plant two other mid-season diploids nearby to be safe.

climate.best_climates: Cool, relatively dry East Anglian conditions and similar cool temperate lowlands with a long autumn.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions are likely to give poorer colour and keeping; very short seasons may not mature a mid-October apple.

health.other: Reported to have some resistance to scab and mildew; other diseases not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A robust heritage cooker for East Anglia and similar climates; give it room as it grows strongly. Pick in mid October, store cool and use it through to early summer.

varieties.name: Norfolk Royal Russet

origin.parentage: Russeted sport of Norfolk Royal

varieties.history: A russeted sport of Norfolk Royal, found in the Burnham Overy Staithe garden of RAF chaplain Rev. C. E. Wright. It entered the National Fruit Collection in 1973 and was released commercially by Highfields Nursery, Gloucester, in 1983. It is now a favourite in East Anglian farm shops. The parent, Norfolk Royal, was a chance seedling found at Wright's Nurseries, North Walsham, around 1908.

look.description: Shaped like Norfolk Royal but largely covered in golden-brown russet, with a warm red flush glowing through on the sunny side; a very handsome apple.

taste.summary: A sweet, pear-like russet with the classic English russet richness and enough acidity to stay lively; tasters rank it among the best-flavoured russets. The flesh is soft and slightly chewy, a little dry but less spongy than Egremont Russet, and it is a short keeper of two to three weeks.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Dec; good from the tree, keeps a few weeks

tree.notes: A spur-bearer of average vigour that crops regularly. Behaves like its parent Norfolk Royal.

pollination.notes: The East of England Apples & Orchards Project lists it in group D (4), while Orange Pippin gives group 3. It is not self-fertile, so a group 3 or 4 partner covers both.

climate.best_climates: Cool, fairly dry eastern England and similar mild temperate regions.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot climates. Like other russets it may lose flavour and texture in heat.

health.other: Good resistance to scab and mildew is reported. The cut flesh browns.

varieties.grow_notes: An excellent russet for gardens in the east and south. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil with a mid-season pollinator, and pick in mid-September.

varieties.name: Norland

origin.parentage: Rescue (a hardy crab hybrid) x Melba

varieties.history: Bred at the federal research station at Morden, Manitoba, by crossing the very hardy Rescue crab with Melba, and released around 1980 for prairie gardens. It is one of the hardiest full-sized eating apples and is grown as far north as Alaska.

look.description: Medium, roundish apple, green to yellow-green with red stripes and flush.

taste.summary: A sweet, juicy summer apple with a light McIntosh-like flavour from its Melba side. Crisp at first but softens within weeks, and the white flesh browns quickly once cut.

tree.notes: A naturally small tree that bears very young, which makes it handy for small northern gardens.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded. Plant another hardy apple or crab that blooms at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Very cold, short-season places - the Canadian prairies, Alaska, northern Minnesota, Scandinavia - where few other apples survive.
climate.poor_climates: Warm temperate regions: the crop ripens in summer heat and turns soft and mealy almost at once. Unsuitable for mild winters.

health.other: Disease resistance not well documented; the main weakness is a short shelf life and quick browning of cut fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant for early fresh eating in the coldest gardens. Pick over a couple of weeks as fruit colours and use it quickly; the small natural size makes netting and picking easy.

varieties.name: Northern Spy

origin.place: East Bloomfield, near Rochester, New York
origin.parentage: Unknown; seedling from seed brought from Salisbury, Connecticut

varieties.history: Grew in the Chapin family's seedling orchard at East Bloomfield, New York, around 1800 and was introduced about 1840. It became a classic northern US pie and storage apple, and its resistance to woolly aphid led East Malling and John Innes to use it as a parent of the MM rootstock series.

look.description: Large, roundish-conical fruit with thin skin, green-yellow under pinkish-red flush and stripes.

taste.summary: Crisp, very juicy, fine-grained flesh with a brisk, roughly even sweet-tart balance and a rich aroma; one grower picks out vanilla notes. It keeps three months or more and holds its shape and tang when baked, which is why it is a classic North American pie apple.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar; improves after a month in store

tree.notes: Very vigorous and notoriously slow to come into bearing on strong roots (sometimes 8-10 years); use a dwarfing rootstock. Tends to fall into alternate-year cropping, so thin in heavy years.

pollination.notes: Late flowering (group 5), which helps it miss spring frosts; needs a late-flowering diploid partner.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental climates such as upstate New York, Michigan and Ontario, where it is winter-hardy and colours well in cool autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid or low-chill regions where fire blight is severe and colour is poor; in cool British summers the very late fruit may struggle to ripen fully.

health.other: Very susceptible to fire blight and prone to bitter pit; thin skin bruises easily. Resistant to woolly aphid.

varieties.grow_notes: Graft onto a dwarfing rootstock to bring it into bearing sooner, and plant with another late-flowering variety. Best where winters are cold and autumns long; thin heavy crops to limit biennial bearing.

varieties.name: Nuvar Cheerfull Gold

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: A modern English dessert apple released by the developer Nuvar, tested under the code NC1, from a conventional Cox x Golden Delicious cross. One database gives a 1979 date, which may refer to the original cross rather than its release; it was marketed as a Cox-style apple with better storage.

look.description: Appearance not well documented; one database records the fruit colour as red despite the name.

taste.summary: A balanced sweet-sharp apple with a pleasant tang. It lacks the layered aromatics of Cox but has crisper flesh, closer to Golden Delicious, and keeps well.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Feb; stores for three months or more

tree.notes: Reported as fairly vigorous, precocious and heavy cropping, and a tip-bearer, so prune lightly and avoid shortening every shoot.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4; pair with another group 3-5 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Temperate south-east England, where it was developed; its Golden Delicious side suggests it tolerates warmer summers better than Cox.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in very cold or hot climates; fruit is reported to hang on the tree into winter, which needs a frost-free autumn.

health.other: Disease resistance described only as average; no detailed data.

varieties.grow_notes: A late keeper for gardens in southern Britain. As a tip-bearer it suits a free-standing bush or half-standard better than tightly pruned cordons; pair with a group 4 partner.

varieties.name: Nuvar Golden Hills

origin.parentage: Recorded as Greensleeves x Greensleeves (a Greensleeves seedling)

varieties.history: One of the 'Nuvar' series of garden apples raised in Kent in the 1980s by John Breach and Hugh Ermen, the breeder also behind Scrumptious and Herefordshire Russet. It is derived from Greensleeves and was selected as a sweeter, more golden version of that apple.

look.description: Clear golden-yellow apple, more yellow than Greensleeves, occasionally with a faint pink cheek.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy with a sweet, fairly rich flavour; a little sweeter than its Greensleeves parent.

tree.notes: Little published growing data. Its Greensleeves parent is compact, very precocious and heavy cropping, which may carry through, but this is unconfirmed.

pollination.notes: Needs a pollinator. Flowering group not recorded; Greensleeves itself is usually listed in group 3.

climate.best_climates: Southern England and similar cool, moist temperate climates where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside the UK; climate values are inferred from English breeding and its parent.

health.other: Disease behaviour not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A garden variety for a sunny spot in southern Britain; pick when the skin turns from green-yellow to full gold. Plant near another mid-season flowering apple.

varieties.name: Opal

origin.place: Institute of Experimental Botany, Czech Republic
origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Topaz
origin.raised_by: Jaroslav Tupý, Institute of Experimental Botany (Czech Academy of Sciences)

varieties.history: Bred in the Czech Republic by Jaroslav Tupý's team at the Institute of Experimental Botany from a Golden Delicious x Topaz cross (1991 per German sources), and protected in the USA and EU in 2005-06. Marketed as Opal, it is grown mostly in Washington State and in several European countries. Not the same as the older English apple 'Opal' (Seabrook, Essex, 1930s).

look.description: Bright yellow to yellow-orange skin, sometimes lightly russeted, on a Golden Delicious-like fruit.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy and sweet with a tangy edge; the fine cream-yellow flesh has a quince-like fragrance with a hint of pear. It barely browns when cut thanks to low polyphenol oxidase.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Feb; ready about two weeks after picking

tree.notes: Medium vigour with a weak central leader, good branching, dense foliage and short fruiting wood.

pollination.notes: UK flowering group not published; plant with another diploid.

climate.best_climates: Continental and temperate Europe and dry sunny regions such as central Washington; as a yellow apple it does not depend on cool nights for colour.
climate.poor_climates: Very short seasons where an early-October apple will not ripen; russeting may be worse in humid conditions.

health.other: Rvi6 (Vf) scab resistance inherited from Topaz and reported tolerance of fire blight; skin may russet.

varieties.grow_notes: A low-spray option for scab-prone areas. Ripens with Golden Delicious, so it needs a reasonably warm, sunny site in the UK. Give the weak central leader support while young.

varieties.name: Opalescent
varieties.history: An American apple introduced in 1899 by the nursery firm McNary & Gaines of Xenia, Ohio; its true origin and parentage are not recorded. The name refers to the waxy skin, which polishes to a high, almost reflective shine. It is a parent of Shenandoah.

look.description: Large, somewhat ribbed conical apple, striped and flushed red over pale yellow, with a greasy skin that takes a glossy polish.

taste.summary: Thin-skinned, juicy and just crisp enough, with a sweet flavour balanced by a fair tartness. Growers single out a delicate floral character, some likening it to lilac, and compare the overall taste with Mutsu or Crispin. Used for baking as well as eating.

tree.notes: Reported to be very productive; little other modern growing data.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering diploid; pair with a group 2-4 partner.

climate.best_climates: Its home range is the American Midwest and mid-Atlantic, with warm summers and cold winters.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in very cold or subtropical regions; the fruit is said to ripen quickly and not travel well.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage curiosity for collectors of old American apples. Give it a sunny site and a mid-season pollinator, and use the fruit promptly as it does not keep long.

varieties.name: Orin

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x Indo
origin.raised_by: Otsuki, an apple grower in Fukushima Prefecture

varieties.history: Raised by a grower named Otsuki in Fukushima Prefecture from Golden Delicious and the Japanese apple Indo, the same parents as Mutsu. The seedling dates from the 1940s (the National Fruit Collection says before 1942) and it was named around 1952; it remains a popular yellow apple in Japan.

look.description: Large, greenish-yellow fruit with conspicuous pale lenticel dots and at most a faint orange cheek.

taste.summary: Very sweet and honeyed with almost no acidity, aromatic and juicy; some tasters also find tropical-fruit overtones. The flesh is firm with a soft, Honeycrisp-like crunch. Admirers love its fragrance; those who like a sharp apple may find it flat.

tree.notes: Average vigour; one source describes it as a tip-bearer. Ploidy is disputed: the National Fruit Collection lists it as triploid, while Japanese growers commonly use it as a pollinizer, which implies diploid.

pollination.notes: UK flowering group not published (it flowered early in the Brogdale records). Ploidy uncertain, so plant two compatible diploids nearby.

climate.best_climates: Humid temperate climates with warm summers and long autumns, like its native Tohoku region of Japan.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, short-season areas, including much of Britain, where a late-October apple may not ripen or sweeten fully.

health.other: Disease behaviour outside Japan not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs a warm, sheltered, sunny spot in Britain to ripen its very late fruit. Leave it on the tree as long as autumn weather allows, then store cool.

varieties.name: Orleans Reinette
varieties.history: Thought to be French and first described in 1776. It won RHS Awards of Merit in 1914 (as 'Winter Ribston') and 1921, and English connoisseurs such as Edward Bunyard ranked it among the finest winter dessert apples.

look.description: Medium, flattish fruit, golden yellow with a warm orange-red flush on the sunny side and a light netting of russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-textured flesh that is not especially juicy but carries a rich, sweet, nutty and aromatic flavour with balancing acidity, close to Blenheim Orange and often compared with Ashmead's Kernel. One taster found a mango-like note after a week or so in store. Valued for flavour rather than crunch; it keeps its shape when cooked.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous spur-bearer with some tendency to alternate cropping. Usually listed as triploid, so it is a poor pollen donor.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4. As a triploid it needs two other diploid pollinators in groups 3-5 and will not pollinate them in return.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sunny sites in southern England and continental Europe; it is widely grown in France and Germany.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, wet sites where scab is severe and late fruit ripens poorly.

health.other: Reported as susceptible to scab; triploid.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in a warm, sunny position for the best flavour, with two diploid partners because it is triploid. Pick in mid October and eat through mid-winter.

varieties.name: Otava

origin.place: Institute of Experimental Botany, Strizovice, Czech Republic
origin.parentage: Reported as Sampion x Jolana (not independently verified)
origin.raised_by: Institute of Experimental Botany, Czech Academy of Sciences

varieties.history: One of the scab-resistant dessert apples from the Czech breeding programme that also produced Topaz and Rajka, aimed at low-spray and organic growing. Detailed release information is not readily available in English-language sources.

look.description: Yellow apple with a light orange cheek; detailed descriptions are scarce.

taste.summary: Usually described as a sweet, juicy yellow apple with mild acidity, keeping well into late winter. Independent tasting notes are limited.

tree.notes: Growth data not well documented in English sources.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; assume a mid-season partner is needed.

climate.best_climates: Central European and British temperate climates, especially damp areas where its scab resistance pays off.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or low-chill regions.

health.other: Bred for scab resistance (Vf gene); other disease behaviour not well documented. Vf resistance has been overcome by new scab races in some regions.

varieties.grow_notes: A good candidate for low-spray gardens in wetter areas thanks to its scab resistance. Plant with a mid-season partner and store the fruit cool for winter eating.

varieties.name: Oxford Conquest

origin.parentage: Blenheim Orange x Court Pendu Plat

varieties.history: Raised in 1927 at Eynsham near Oxford by the amateur breeder F.W. Wastie, who also raised several other Oxfordshire apples. It crosses two classic late apples, Blenheim Orange and Court Pendu Plat, and survives mainly in collections.

look.description: Medium-large, broadly conical fruit, green-yellow with a dull brownish flush and almost no russet.

taste.summary: The National Fruit Collection describes rather tough flesh with an acid flavour; little else is recorded, so it is best seen as a sharp, firm late apple.

tree.notes: No published growing data. Note that Blenheim Orange, one parent, is triploid, so the ploidy of this seedling cannot be assumed.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; it flowers early-to-mid season at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions like its Oxfordshire home.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance outside England.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A local-history apple for Oxfordshire collections. Grow it as a typical English late dessert apple in a sunny, sheltered spot, and plant other varieties nearby until its pollination needs are known.

varieties.name: Palmer's Rosey

origin.place: Garden of H.T. Palmer, Whyteleafe, Surrey, England

varieties.history: A Surrey garden apple that arose with H.T. Palmer at Whyteleafe and was sent to the National Fruit Trials in 1965. It survives mainly through the National Fruit Collection at Brogdale.

look.description: Flattish-round apple with a pale whitish-yellow skin, about half covered in striped and mottled orange-red to bright red.

taste.summary: Crisp, fairly tender flesh with a noticeably aromatic flavour for an August apple.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, straight from the tree

tree.notes: No published growing data.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records it in full flower at much the same time as Cox, so group 3 is a reasonable working assumption.

climate.best_climates: South-east England and comparable cool maritime climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not grown outside England; climate values are inferred from its origin.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A rare local variety for collectors of early English apples. Treat it as a typical spur-bearing dessert apple and plant with a group 2-4 partner.

varieties.name: Pancake Apple
varieties.history: Offered in Britain as a cooking apple, but no variety of this name (nor a synonym) appears in the National Fruit Collection register or the other pomological sources consulted. Its origin and identity are unconfirmed; it may be a local or trade name for another variety.

look.description: Not recorded.

taste.summary: No reliable tasting description found; listed only as a cooking apple.

tree.notes: No growing data found.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; plant with a partner of known mid-season group to be safe.

health.other: Not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Too little is documented to give specific advice; grow as a typical British cooking apple.

varieties.name: Parkland
varieties.history: A very hardy Canadian prairie apple released by the federal research station at Morden, Manitoba, around 1979. It is grown where only the toughest apples and applecrabs survive, including sheltered sites in the far north.

look.description: Small to medium, green ripening to yellow with red stripes and flush.

taste.summary: Soft, sweet and juicy when ripe but rather tart and plain in flavour; best eaten straight off the tree or turned into sauce, since it keeps poorly.

tree.notes: Growers report trees of around 6 m on vigorous roots and generous crops, but tree traits are not formally documented in the sources consulted.

pollination.notes: Plant with another hardy apple or crab for pollination; flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Severe prairie and northern climates with short summers (Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, the Yukon in sheltered spots).
climate.poor_climates: Warm or hot regions, where an August apple bred for the prairies softens and goes over quickly (inferred).

health.other: Disease ratings not documented in the sources consulted; very poor keeping quality is its main limitation.

varieties.grow_notes: A survival apple for very cold gardens. Give it a warm, sheltered spot in the far north, plant a hardy pollinator nearby, and freeze surplus fruit as sauce since it will not store.

varieties.name: Patte de Loup
varieties.history: An old russet from the Beaupréau district of Anjou in the Loire valley, generally dated to the late 1700s, although one French account links it to a description from 1670. 'Wolf's paw' refers to a scar-like line across the russet, as though the fruit had been clawed.

look.description: Flattish, often lopsided fruit almost covered in fawn-brown russet over green, typically marked by a narrow scratch-like scar.

taste.summary: Fine, dense, firm flesh, not especially juicy, with a sweet, gently acid and perfumed flavour carrying a faint aniseed note, in the manner of the French fennel-scented russets. Develops in store through winter.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar, after a period in store

tree.notes: Vigorous, upright and fruitful; fruit holds firmly on the branch, so it tolerates windy sites.

pollination.notes: Mid-to-late flowering; French sources suggest Golden Delicious as a partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild Atlantic-influenced western France and southern England, with a long autumn to finish this late apple.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or cold-autumn areas may not ripen it fully before frost.

health.other: French sources report good resistance to scab and pests; little UK data.

varieties.grow_notes: A late keeping russet for a sunny, sheltered garden in the south. Pick in late October and store cool and slightly humid so the russet skin does not shrivel; eat from midwinter.

varieties.name: Peasgood's Nonsuch

origin.parentage: Seedling of Catshead, pollen parent unknown

varieties.history: Raised by Mrs Peasgood of Stamford, Lincolnshire, from a pip sown around 1858. It won a First Class Certificate from the Royal Horticultural Society in 1872 and became a Victorian show-bench favourite for its sheer size; it is a parent of Charles Ross and Rev. W. Wilks.

look.description: Very large, broad, handsome fruit, greenish-yellow to gold with carmine-orange stripes and flush and a few russet dots.

taste.summary: Tender, slightly coarse, moderately juicy flesh with a gentle sweet-sharp flavour that is pleasant raw. Its real strength is cooking: it breaks down into a sweet, smooth puree needing little sugar, ideal for baked apples and sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Nov for cooking; raw from late Sep

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and spreading; cropping is fair rather than heavy. Thin clusters to one fruit for the largest apples.

pollination.notes: Needs a diploid partner in group 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Cool, fairly dry eastern and southern England, where its Victorian reputation was made.
climate.poor_climates: Wet western districts encourage the scab and canker it is prone to; hot summers are untested.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and canker; avoid wet, poorly drained sites.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on well-drained, fertile soil in an open spot with good air flow to keep scab and canker down. Pair with a group 3 partner and thin hard for exhibition-size fruit.

varieties.name: Peck's Pleasant
varieties.history: A New England heirloom thought to come from Rhode Island and recorded by 1832. Nineteenth-century American pomologists rated it highly as a winter dessert apple, but it was never widely planted commercially.

look.description: Medium, flattish fruit, green ripening to clear bright yellow with an orange-red to pinkish blush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Tender, crisp yellowish flesh with a sweet, mildly acidic and highly aromatic flavour; nineteenth-century American writers rated it very good to best for winter eating. Modern opinion is more mixed, with at least one grower finding only a green, grassy taste.

tree.notes: Little modern growing data.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; it flowers in the middle of the season at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: New England and similar humid temperate climates with warm summers and long autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons may not ripen it fully; hot, low-chill climates are unsuitable.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Pick late and store cool, and it will keep its aroma into early spring. Plant with a mid-season partner in a warm, sunny spot.

varieties.name: Pepin Shafranny

origin.parentage: Orleans Reinette x (Pepinka Litovskaya x Kitaika, Malus prunifolia)

varieties.history: One of Ivan Michurin's best-known apples, raised in 1907 by crossing Orleans Reinette with his own hybrid of the Lithuanian Pepinka and the Chinese crab Kitaika. It entered the Soviet state register in 1947 and was zoned across much of Russia, including western and eastern Siberia; it is a parent of later Russian varieties such as Krasnyi Shtandart.

look.description: Small to medium, neat and symmetrical round-conical apple, greenish-yellow under a diffuse dark red blush with darker stripes and many small white dots.

taste.summary: Dense, juicy cream flesh with a winey sweetness and a delicate spicy fragrance. Keeps its quality well into late winter and is highly regarded in Russia for jam.

tree.notes: Medium-sized tree whose crown becomes broad and very dense, with drooping branches; much of the crop is borne on young shoots and short spurs. Needs regular thinning-out pruning, or the fruit stays small and tends to drop. Trees damaged in hard winters regenerate well.

pollination.notes: Brogdale records it flowering early, alongside White Transparent. Russian sources rate it highly self-fertile, though a partner improves set.

climate.best_climates: Central Russian climates with cold winters and warm summers; it has been grown as far east as Siberia.
climate.poor_climates: The harshest northern winters, where it is only moderately hardy by Russian standards; little information from mild or hot climates.

health.other: Russian trials rate fruit and leaves moderately susceptible to scab (Brogdale describes it as scab-resistant); moderately susceptible to codling moth.

varieties.grow_notes: A heavy-cropping winter apple for cold gardens. Prune every year to open the crown and keep fruit size up. Brogdale lists a much earlier picking time (late August) than Russian sources, so judge ripeness by taste and seed colour.

varieties.name: Pig's Nose Pippin
varieties.history: Thought to come from Herefordshire and first described in 1884. It is preserved in the National Fruit Collection and by Marcher Apple Network collections; it is not the same as the separate variety 'Pig's Snout'.

look.description: Smallish, conical fruit, yellow with orange stripes and a little russet.

taste.summary: Fine-grained, crisp cream flesh with a sweet flavour. Few other tasting details are recorded.

tree.notes: No published growing data.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; it flowers mid-season at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: The Welsh Marches and other mild, moist western British counties where it originated.
climate.poor_climates: No record outside Britain.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A local heritage apple for Herefordshire and Marches orchards. Plant with mid-season partners and treat it as a typical spur-bearing dessert apple.

varieties.name: Pilot

origin.parentage: Clivia x Undine

varieties.history: A late-keeping dessert apple from the East German fruit research institute at Dresden-Pillnitz, released in 1988 and a half-sibling of Pinova through its parent Clivia. Not to be confused with the old American 'Pilot', a nineteenth-century Virginia seedling.

look.description: Medium fruit with a yellow to orange ground covered up to about two-thirds in strong cinnabar red; the skin is rather rough and tough, so it bruises little.

taste.summary: Firm, juicy flesh with a sweet-sharp, fairly brisk flavour that becomes sweeter and more aromatic after a few months in store. A true winter keeper rather than an apple for picking and eating.
taste.best_eaten: Jan-May; not ready until after Christmas

tree.notes: Reported to crop early and heavily on dwarfing stocks and to be easy to grow; detailed habit data are scarce in English sources.

pollination.notes: UK flowering group not published; plant with another diploid.

climate.best_climates: Central European fruit regions with cold winters and moderate summers, and by extension most of lowland Britain.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, short-winter climates are untested; very short seasons may not mature a mid-October apple.

health.other: Low susceptibility to scab, powdery mildew and fire blight is reported, making it suitable for most apple-growing sites.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for anyone wanting home-grown apples into spring: pick in October, store cool and start eating in the new year. Its disease tolerance suits low-spray gardens.

varieties.name: Pink Pearl

origin.parentage: Seedling of Surprise, a red-fleshed apple

varieties.history: Bred by the Californian plant breeder Albert Etter at Ettersburg from the red-fleshed apple Surprise, and introduced in 1944 as the pick of his red-fleshed seedlings. It remains one of the best-known pink-fleshed apples.

look.description: Medium, conical fruit with translucent creamy pale green-yellow skin, a soft pink blush and striking bright pink flesh; the blossom is also pink.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, bright pink flesh with a very tart flavour lifted by just enough sweetness; tasters compare it to pink grapefruit or sweet lemonade, and one notes a touch of tannin. Almost a cooker in acidity, it makes attractive pink sauce and juice but keeps only two to three weeks.

tree.notes: Weak-growing and a light, rather biennial cropper; put it on a moderately vigorous rootstock and thin heavy crops.

pollination.notes: Listed as very early flowering (group 1) in one database; choose an early-flowering pollinator. Pink blossom is ornamental.

climate.best_climates: Mild coastal climates like northern California and the Pacific Northwest, and other temperate regions with moderate winters.
climate.poor_climates: Humid, disease-prone regions where its poor disease resistance shows; early bloom risks spring frost damage.

health.other: Rated as having poor overall disease resistance; early blossom can be caught by frost.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in a frost-free, sunny spot with an early-flowering pollinator and good air flow to limit disease. Eat or cook the fruit soon after picking.

varieties.name: Pinova

origin.parentage: Clivia (Geheimrat Dr. Oldenburg x Cox's Orange Pippin) x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: Bred at the fruit research institute at Dresden-Pillnitz in what was then East Germany from a 1965 cross, and released in 1986. It is grown across Europe and sold in the USA as Piñata and in France as Corail.

look.description: Golden Delicious shape with orange-red stripes and flush over a yellow ground.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy and fairly tender, with an intense sweet flavour balanced by enough tartness; several tasters notice a floral scent reminiscent of roses. It shows its Cox ancestry and keeps three months or more without losing quality.

tree.notes: Rather weak-growing spur-bearer that crops heavily and regularly; suits small trees and intensive systems.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4. Sources disagree on its value as a pollen donor (one rates it poor, another good), so add a reliable pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Temperate central and western Europe, including mild damp climates, and sunny fruit regions with warm rather than hot summers; blossom has some frost resistance.
climate.poor_climates: Very hot summers are likely to reduce colour and storage quality; short-season northern sites may not ripen it.

health.other: Generally good disease resistance with some resistance to scab and canker; somewhat susceptible to powdery mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: A reliable, compact garden apple for warmer parts of the UK. Thin heavy crops for size, keep mildew in check in spring, and plant with a group 3-5 pollinator.

varieties.name: Pitmaston Pine Apple

origin.parentage: Seedling, thought to be of Golden Pippin
origin.raised_by: Mr White, steward to Lord Foley; introduced by John Williams of Pitmaston, Worcester

varieties.history: Raised around 1785 by Mr White, steward to Lord Foley at Witley in Worcestershire, probably from a Golden Pippin pip. The Worcester nurseryman John Williams of Pitmaston later introduced it, and it is still sought after for its unusual flavour.

look.description: Small, neat, narrowly conical fruit, golden yellow with a fine coat of light russet.

taste.summary: A small yellow apple whose firm, juicy, never-mealy flesh is sweet but lively, with a prominent musky, pineapple-like flavour that tasters also call sherbet-like; honeyed and nutty notes add richness. Best eaten within two or three weeks of picking.

tree.notes: Prone to biennial bearing, with heavy crops in the 'on' year; thinning helps both regularity and fruit size.

pollination.notes: Usually placed in flowering group 3; pair with a group 2-4 diploid.

climate.best_climates: Sheltered, sunny sites in southern and western England, where its small fruit sweetens fully.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, exposed sites give small, sharp fruit; not documented in hot climates.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded; the main problem is biennial bearing and small fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: Thin heavy crops early to keep the tree cropping every year and the fruit a usable size. Give it a warm spot and a group 3 partner.

varieties.name: Pixie

origin.place: National Fruit Trials, RHS Garden Wisley, Surrey, England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin or Sunset x unknown

varieties.history: Raised in 1947 at the National Fruit Trials at Wisley, probably from a seedling of Cox or Sunset. It received an RHS First Class Certificate in 1972 and holds the Award of Garden Merit as a reliable, healthy garden apple.

look.description: Small, flattish, Cox-like apple, yellow with an orange-red flush and streaks and a little russet.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy cream flesh with an intense, Cox-style aromatic flavour, sharper and more refreshing than Cox when first picked and mellowing in store.

tree.notes: Easy, regular cropper that tends to set too many fruits, which then stay small; thin after flowering. Does well on dwarfing rootstocks such as M27 and M9.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4; any group 3-5 diploid will pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens across Britain and north-west Europe; more forgiving of damp than Cox because of its disease resistance.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to soften the fruit and reduce its sharp-aromatic balance.

health.other: Good resistance to scab and mildew. Main fault is overcropping, giving small fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best Cox-style apples for small gardens: healthy, compact on dwarfing stocks and reliable. Thin fruitlets hard and store the crop in a cool place for eating after Christmas.

varieties.name: Polka

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: Wijcik McIntosh x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: One of the 'Ballerina' columnar apples bred at East Malling from the compact Wijcik sport of McIntosh; raised in 1976 and released in 1989. Polka is the trade name, and the national collection records it under the cultivar name Trajan.

look.description: Medium apple with a dark red flush over green.

taste.summary: Sweet, crisp and juicy with a mild, McIntosh-family character that some compare to Spartan. A pleasant eater rather than a complex one; it does not keep long.

tree.notes: Grows as a narrow single column with short fruiting spurs, needing almost no pruning; ideal for pots and very small spaces.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; pair with another early-to-mid diploid, such as another Ballerina.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens such as the UK and northern Europe, where it was bred and tested.
climate.poor_climates: Little evidence from hot-summer regions; McIntosh-type colour and texture usually suffer in heat.

health.other: Disease resistance described as average; specific ratings not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow in a large container or a sunny border where space is tight; keep the leader single and simply remove any side shoots that grow long. Feed and water well, as columnar trees in pots dry out quickly.

varieties.name: Polly
varieties.history: A Cornish apple sent to the National Fruit Trials in 1954; nothing more is known of its origin. Not to be confused with Polly Prosser (a Cox seedling) or the Somerset apple Polly Whitehair.

look.description: Broad, rounded-conical apple with a greenish-yellow skin and little or no russet.

taste.summary: Soft white flesh with a sweet, gently acidic flavour; usable both raw and in the kitchen.

tree.notes: No published growing data.

pollination.notes: Brogdale flowering dates are close to Cox, so group 3 is assumed.

climate.best_climates: Mild, wet south-west England, where it originated; likely suited to other mild maritime areas.
climate.poor_climates: No records outside the UK; climate values are inferred from origin.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded, though Cornish local varieties are often chosen for tolerance of damp conditions.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a heritage collection in the south-west. Use the fruit promptly as the flesh softens quickly; plant with a group 2-4 partner.

varieties.name: Polly Prosser

origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Duke of Devonshire

varieties.history: Raised in Maidstone, Kent, in 1946 by J.H. Cooper from Cox crossed with the late-keeping Duke of Devonshire. It is held in the National Fruit Collection but is little known outside heritage collections.

look.description: Medium-large, flattish, slightly ribbed fruit, green-yellow with orange streaks.

taste.summary: Firm, rather coarse yellowish-white flesh with a sweet, mildly acidic and rich flavour. Few further tasting notes are published.

tree.notes: No published growing data.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not published; it flowers mid-season at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: South-east England, where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance elsewhere.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded; its Cox parent often passes on canker and mildew susceptibility.

varieties.grow_notes: A Kentish heritage apple for collectors. Grow it like Cox, in a sheltered sunny site with good drainage, and plant a mid-season pollinator nearby.

varieties.name: Pomme Gris

origin.place: St Lawrence valley, Quebec (French Canada); possibly derived from a French grey reinette

varieties.history: An old russet apple of French Canada, long grown around Montreal and the St Lawrence and thought by some to descend from a French grey reinette. It was among the apples planted by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and remains a heritage favourite in north-eastern North America.

look.description: Small, flattish apple covered in grey-brown to golden russet.

taste.summary: A rich, sweet, nutty russet with firm, fine flesh and a sprightly finish; improves for a few weeks after picking.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well recorded.

pollination.notes: Pollination details not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter north-eastern North America (Quebec, New England, New York); also grown historically in Virginia.
climate.poor_climates: No reliable reports; very warm, low-chill regions are unlikely to suit it.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A hardy heritage russet for cold gardens. Plant with another diploid that flowers at a similar time and store the fruit cool to bring out its flavour.

varieties.name: Porter's Perfection

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: Associated with Charles Porter of East Lambrook in south Somerset and introduced in the early 1900s. A late bittersharp valued for blending and occasionally for single-variety cider.

look.description: Conical fruit with a pale cream ground mostly covered by a dark red flush.

taste.summary: A bittersharp with high acid and fairly mild tannin; tart if picked early or grown in a cool spot, it needs a few weeks of storage before milling.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; store about a month, then mill Dec.

tree.notes: Vigorous, heavy-cropping tree with some tendency to alternate years.

pollination.notes: Needs a compatible pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp maritime climates with long autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season regions; the very late fruit needs a long autumn.

health.other: Generally healthy, with some resistance to scab and canker.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the last cider apples to pick; let the fruit mellow in store before pressing. A good source of acid to balance bittersweets.

varieties.name: Prairie Spy

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Not firmly recorded. One source gives Wealthy x Northwestern Greening; Northern Spy ancestry has been suggested but not confirmed.

varieties.history: Grown from seed planted in 1914 at the University of Minnesota fruit breeding farm, selected in 1923 as Minnesota 1007 and named in 1940. The name borrows from Northern Spy, but its parentage remains uncertain.

look.description: Large, roundish apple with a yellow ground streaked and flushed red.

taste.summary: Firm, dense, crisp flesh with a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavour that improves after some weeks in store. Excellent for baking and pies, and one of the longest keepers among hardy apples.
taste.best_eaten: Nov-Mar, after a few weeks in store

tree.notes: Slow to start bearing - expect several years - but crops well once established.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded; needs a compatible diploid pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cold northern climates (zone 3-5) with a long enough autumn to ripen a late apple, such as Minnesota and the northern Great Lakes.
climate.poor_climates: Very short seasons where a late apple will not mature, and hot or mild-winter regions where it lacks chill and colours poorly.

health.other: Generally reported as healthy, but specific scab and fire blight ratings are not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Be patient: plant it on a dwarfing rootstock if you want fruit sooner. Leave fruit on the tree as long as frosts allow, then store cold for winter baking.

varieties.name: Primrose Pippin

origin.parentage: Seedling from the Keepers Nursery programme (seedling 82); parents not published

varieties.history: Karim Habibi's best-regarded seedling so far, named after his eldest child. It was shown to the RHS Fruit Group in 2023 and was released for ordering in May 2025. It is sold under the trademark Primrose Pippin. As yet it has only been grown in Kent.

look.description: Yellow skin that develops a red striped flush late in the season; roughly round-oblong with a long thin stalk.

taste.summary: A modern-style crisp, juicy apple with more sugar (about 18% by refractometer), acidity and fruitiness than most late-season supermarket types. The raiser and the RHS fruit specialist Joan Morgan both describe the balance as excellent.

tree.notes: No published growing data found.

pollination.notes: Self-sterile; group 3 (C in nursery lists).

climate.best_climates: Only trialled in Kent so far.
climate.poor_climates: Not yet known; a mid-November pick needs a long season.

health.other: No significant fungal susceptibility seen in Kent trials; not yet tested elsewhere.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant with another group 2-4 apple. Because it ripens very late, give it the warmest, most sheltered spot you have.

varieties.name: Priscilla

origin.place: Purdue University, Lafayette, Indiana (PRI co-operative programme)
origin.parentage: Starking Delicious x PRI 610-2 (Vf scab resistance from Malus floribunda)

varieties.history: One of the earliest releases (1972) of the Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois programme that bred scab resistance from a Japanese flowering crab into dessert apples. It was intended as a disease-resistant apple with some Delicious character.

look.description: Waxy, bright red blush over a yellow ground, slightly conical in the Delicious manner.

taste.summary: Crisp, fairly juicy flesh with a sweet but noticeably tart flavour that varies from year to year; descriptions range from mild and Delicious-like to pleasantly sharp. Good fresh off the tree, it also holds its shape when baked, makes a pink-tinged sauce and keeps one to two months.

tree.notes: Average vigour with a spreading, flat-topped habit; regular cropper suited to beginners and organic growers.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; plant with another group 2-4 variety.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates of the eastern and midwestern US where scab, rust and fire blight are routine problems.
climate.poor_climates: Little documented performance in hot, low-chill or very cool maritime regions.

health.other: Scab-immune (Vf) and very resistant to fire blight and cedar-apple rust; some susceptibility to canker.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable low-spray apple for the home garden. Give it full sun and a mid-season pollinator; chill and hardiness figures are estimates from where it is grown.

varieties.name: Pristine

origin.place: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana (PRI co-operative programme)
origin.parentage: Camuzat x Co-op 10; scab resistance (Vf) traces back to Malus floribunda 821

varieties.history: Released in 1994 by the joint Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) disease-resistance breeding programme after testing as Co-op 32. It was aimed at providing a scab-immune early yellow apple to replace older summer varieties.

look.description: Clear, glossy lemon-yellow apple, sometimes with a faint warm blush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy, firm yellow flesh that is Granny Smith-tart if picked a few weeks early, mellowing at full ripeness to a gentle tartness with sweetness beneath; one grower notes a pear-like flavour with a citrus bite. Unusually good for such an early apple but best eaten within a week or two; also good for sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, within a week or two of picking

tree.notes: Fruit ripens over an extended period, so pick in several passes. Thin to discourage alternate bearing.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4; needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates of the US Midwest and East, where an early scab-immune apple is valuable.
climate.poor_climates: Its short shelf life limits it everywhere; little evidence of performance in hot, low-chill regions.

health.other: Scab-immune (Vf); some resistance to mildew but only moderate tolerance of fire blight and cedar-apple rust.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-spray summer apple: plant in sun with a mid-to-late flowering partner and harvest in stages. Eat or process quickly as it does not keep.

varieties.name: Profusion

origin.parentage: Usually given as Malus 'Lemoinei' x Malus sieboldii

varieties.history: A Dutch purple-leaved crab from the Boskoop nursery district, introduced in the late 1930s and widely planted in Europe and North America for its wine-red spring blossom. Improved selections are sold as 'Profusion Improved'.

look.description: Tiny ox-blood red fruits about 1.5 cm, on long stalks in clusters, persisting on the tree into winter.

taste.summary: Grown purely for ornament; the tiny fruit is sharp and is mostly left for birds or added in small amounts to mixed crab jelly for colour.
taste.best_eaten: Not an eating apple; display Sep-Dec

tree.notes: Young leaves are purple, maturing to bronze-green; deep wine-red flowers fade to pink. Grows to roughly 3-5 m after ten years.

pollination.notes: Long flowering period with abundant pollen; a good partner for early-flowering apples.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates of north-west Europe and the northern US, in open, airy sites.
climate.poor_climates: Damp, sheltered sites where scab and mildew build up on the foliage.

health.other: Some susceptibility to canker and powdery mildew, and scab can spoil the leaves in wet seasons.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in an open, sunny position with good air flow to keep leaf disease down. Its early, long blossom makes it a useful pollinator for early-flowering apples.

varieties.name: Queen Cox

origin.place: Appleby Fruit Farm, Kingston Bagpuize, Berkshire (now Oxfordshire), England
origin.parentage: Colour sport of Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: A more highly coloured clone of Cox's Orange Pippin, found at Appleby Fruit Farm, Kingston Bagpuize, and received by the National Fruit Trials in 1953. It became one of the standard commercial Cox clones. A separate self-fertile selection is sold under a similar name.

look.description: Typical Cox shape and russet freckling, but more of the skin is covered by a deeper orange-red flush and stripes than in standard Cox.

taste.summary: Like Cox, with firm, juicy, slightly acid flesh and a rich, aromatic flavour that brings floral, pear-drop and honeyed notes into balance. It improves for a few weeks after picking.

tree.notes: Grows and crops like ordinary Cox: a spur-bearer of medium vigour that needs good soil, shelter and attentive disease control.

pollination.notes: Flowers with Cox in group 3. Standard Queen Cox needs a pollinator; only the separately sold self-fertile selection can set fruit alone. Good partners include Egremont Russet, Discovery and Worcester Pearmain.

climate.best_climates: Warm, sheltered sites in southern England and similar cool-summer maritime climates on well-drained soil.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, wet districts encourage canker and scab, and hot summers give poorly coloured, soft fruit with less aroma.

health.other: Shares Cox's weaknesses: canker, scab and mildew, along with some bitter pit and cracking.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it as you would Cox: a sunny, sheltered site on fertile, free-draining soil, with spraying or careful hygiene against scab and mildew. Choose it over standard Cox mainly for better colour.

varieties.name: Rajka

origin.place: Institute of Experimental Botany, Strizovice, Czech Republic
origin.parentage: Sampion x a scab-resistant selection (given as Katka in some sources, Jolana x Rubin in others)
origin.raised_by: Institute of Experimental Botany, Czech Academy of Sciences

varieties.history: Bred at the Czech Institute of Experimental Botany (the programme that also gave Topaz) for resistance to apple scab; the cross dates from the early 1980s and it was released in the 1990s. Through its Sampion parent it descends from Golden Delicious and Lord Lambourne.

look.description: Attractive medium-to-large, roundish-conical fruit almost entirely covered in bright deep red over a yellow ground, with a little russet in the stalk cavity.

taste.summary: Fairly crisp, open-textured cream-yellow flesh that snaps cleanly, with a sweet flavour and good acidity much like Elstar; after a good summer it can carry a hint of strawberry. Juicy and pleasant rather than complex, and it keeps a few weeks.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, spurs freely, comes into bearing early and crops regularly; fruit holds well on the tree. Suited to organic growing.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (group 3) and a good pollinator for other group 2-4 diploids.

climate.best_climates: Central European and British temperate climates, including damp western areas where its scab resistance is a real advantage; suggested as suitable for cooler regions.
climate.poor_climates: Low-chill or very hot regions; warm nights are likely to reduce its strong red colour.

health.other: Scab resistant (Vf) and tolerant of mildew. Birds can damage the fruit. Vf resistance has broken down to new scab races in some regions.
