varieties.grow_notes: An easy, healthy garden apple that needs little spraying, even in wet areas. Plant with a group 2-4 partner, thin if the set is heavy, and pick in early October.

varieties.name: Ralls Janet
varieties.history: A Virginia apple associated with Caleb Ralls's orchard in Amherst County around 1800; one story has Thomas Jefferson passing on scions he received from the French envoy Edmond-Charles Genet. Introduced to Japan around 1870 and renamed Kokko in 1900, it was the backbone of Aomori's apple industry for decades and is the mother of Fuji.

look.description: Medium, roundish to blunt-conical apple, greenish-yellow mottled and streaked with pink to dark red, often with a heavy bloom and a little russet near the stalk.

taste.summary: Dense, crisp, yellowish flesh with a lively sweet-tart balance and a pleasant scent when cut. A long keeper, though it turns mealy by late spring unless cold-stored; also used for pies, apple butter and blending into cider.

tree.notes: Vigorous, wide-spreading tree whose growth slows once in full bearing. Colours poorly and needs a long season to ripen.

pollination.notes: One of the latest apples to blossom (at Brogdale about a week after Golden Delicious; in Japan about five days after Fuji), which lets it escape spring frosts - hence the name Neverfail. Pair with another late-flowering diploid.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm seasons such as Virginia and the American mid-South, and northern Japan, where it was long the main commercial apple.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or very cold areas (considered unsuitable for Hokkaido); poorly drained, acid soils encourage bark disease.

health.other: Very susceptible to blossom fire blight and somewhat to scab and bitter rot, but highly resistant to collar rot. Prone to rough-bark disease on wet, acid soils in Japan.

varieties.grow_notes: A useful apple for frost pockets because it blooms so late, provided the summer is long enough to ripen it. Pick in late October and store cold; avoid it where fire blight is common.

varieties.name: Rave

origin.place: University of Minnesota Horticultural Research Center, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Honeycrisp x MonArk
origin.raised_by: University of Minnesota apple breeding programme (David Bedford, James Luby)

varieties.history: Bred at the University of Minnesota by crossing Honeycrisp with the early Arkansas apple MonArk, and trialled as MN55. It is a managed (licensed) variety: Stemilt in Washington State markets it as Rave from about 2017-18, while Minnesota growers sell the same apple as First Kiss.

look.description: Bright red flush with some streaking over a yellow ground; a Honeycrisp-type look on a smaller, earlier fruit.

taste.summary: Very crisp, shattering, juice-laden flesh in the Honeycrisp mould, with a brighter tart edge than its parent balanced by good sugar. An eating apple only: the flesh collapses when cooked.
taste.best_eaten: Aug-Oct; fresh, or from cold store

tree.notes: Fruit tends to drop before it is fully ripe, so crops need watching and picking promptly. Propagation is restricted under licence, so trees are rarely available to home growers outside Minnesota (where it is sold as First Kiss).

pollination.notes: No published UK flowering group; plant with another apple flowering at the same time.

climate.best_climates: Bred for Minnesota winters and grown commercially in the hot, dry, irrigated orchards of central Washington, where it ripens in midsummer.
climate.poor_climates: Little record outside the northern US; untested in mild maritime climates such as the UK, and its pre-harvest drop is a nuisance anywhere.

health.other: Main documented weakness is pre-harvest fruit drop. Disease ratings not published in the sources checked.

varieties.grow_notes: Mainly a commercial club apple; where trees are available, give it a sunny site and pick over several passes as fruit colours, because ripe apples fall readily. Chill hours and hardiness are estimates from its Minnesota origin.

varieties.name: Raxao
varieties.history: A traditional Asturian cider apple, one of the local varieties approved for the protected 'Sidra de Asturias' designation and characterised by the regional agricultural research service. It is regarded as one of the more valuable varieties for cider making.

look.description: Fairly large, flattened-round fruit, yellow-green with orange-brown and red colouring streaked purple-red; cream flesh.

taste.summary: Belongs to the acid group of Asturian cider apples: a clearly sharp juice with good sugar and only modest phenolics, giving a slight bitter edge. Valued for freshness and acidity in the typical Asturian blend.

tree.notes: Very vigorous and slow to come into bearing; productive once established but strongly inclined to alternate cropping.

pollination.notes: Flowers very late by Asturian standards (early-to-mid May there), which helps it escape spring frost; pair with other late-flowering cider apples.

climate.best_climates: Mild, humid Atlantic climates like the Asturian valleys, with long autumns for its November ripening.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season or early-frost regions where its very late fruit cannot ripen; cold-hardiness untested.

health.other: Low susceptibility to brown rot, canker and mildew in Asturian trials; main drawback is strong biennial bearing.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs space and patience: a big tree that is slow to start. Thin heavily in 'on' years to reduce alternation. Late flowering makes it a good choice for frost-prone valleys.

varieties.name: Red Astrachan

origin.place: Russia (name refers to Astrakhan); reached Sweden from Russia

varieties.history: An old Russian summer apple that was brought to Sweden around 1780, introduced to England in 1816 and to the United States in 1835. Its hardiness and early ripening made it one of the most widely planted summer apples across North America in the 19th century, from New England to the South.

look.description: Medium, flattish fruit washed and streaked deep crimson over pale green-yellow, with a bluish waxy bloom.

taste.summary: Juicy, crisp white flesh, often tinged red, with a brisk tart flavour and some aroma. Good eaten straight from the tree but goes mealy within days; best known as a sauce and pie apple.
taste.best_eaten: Aug, within a few days of picking

tree.notes: Hardy, vigorous and productive. Fruit ripens unevenly over a few weeks and falls readily, so pick in several rounds.

pollination.notes: Early flowering; plant with another early-to-mid season diploid. UK flowering group not confirmed.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter continental climates (Russia, Scandinavia, northern US) and, as an early apple, widely across the eastern US including the South.
climate.poor_climates: Mild, very wet climates encourage scab; low-chill subtropical areas are unsuitable.

health.other: Susceptible to scab and fire blight, and to summer fruit rots; blossom can be frosted.

varieties.grow_notes: A tough, hardy tree for cold sites. Pick over several passes as the fruit colours and use it at once for sauce or pies.

varieties.name: Red Delicious

origin.parentage: Chance seedling of unknown parentage (Yellow Bellflower has been suggested)

varieties.history: Found around 1880 by Jesse Hiatt on his farm near Peru, Iowa, and first called Hawkeye. Stark Brothers bought it and launched it as Delicious in 1895, and it was renamed Red Delicious after they acquired the unrelated Golden Delicious. Repeated selection of ever-redder sports such as Starking made it the leading US apple for most of the 20th century, at some cost to flavour.

look.description: Tall, strongly conical fruit with five prominent bumps at the eye, dark crimson-red over most of the skin (striped in the original, solid in modern sports).

taste.summary: Sweet, juicy flesh with a light crispness, very little acidity and only a faint aroma, sometimes likened to slightly over-ripe melon, under a thick, tough skin. Freshly picked fruit from a warm climate is refreshing, but stored supermarket fruit is often mealy and bland.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; eat fresh, as texture declines in ordinary store

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous; many commercial strains are compact spur types. Precocious and productive.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 4 and a good pollen donor; crab apples and Golden Delicious are common orchard partners.

climate.best_climates: Sunny continental climates with hot days and cool autumn nights, such as central Washington State, where it colours deeply and develops full sweetness.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, cloudy maritime climates such as Britain, where it ripens late, colours poorly and tastes thin; very hot nights also spoil colour.

health.other: Fairly resistant to cedar-apple rust; moderately susceptible to scab. Prone to watercore when left late on the tree.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow it only where summers are warm and sunny; in Britain it is a curiosity rather than a reliable cropper. Plant with a group 4 partner.

varieties.name: Red Falstaff

origin.parentage: Sport of Falstaff (James Grieve x Golden Delicious)

varieties.history: A redder-skinned colour sport of Falstaff, the James Grieve x Golden Delicious apple raised at East Malling. It shares Falstaff's reliability and holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit; details of exactly where and when the sport was found are not well documented.

look.description: Medium, roundish fruit with a bright red to orange-red flush over much of the yellow skin, redder than ordinary Falstaff.

taste.summary: Crisp and very juicy, with a sweet-sharp balance that combines the zest of James Grieve with Golden Delicious sweetness. Good fresh or pressed for juice.

tree.notes: Regular, heavy cropper that can overcrop and give small fruit, so thin in good years. Blossom is relatively frost-resistant.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3. Described as self-fertile, but crops better with a group 2-4 partner; also a good pollinator for others.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate gardens throughout Britain and northern Europe; frost-tolerant blossom makes it useful in colder spots.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions, where fruit is likely to soften quickly and colour less.

health.other: Some susceptibility to scab; Falstaff is generally regarded as fairly healthy and mildew-tolerant.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable garden apple that suits small trees and cordons on dwarfing stocks. Thin fruitlets to keep size up and regular cropping.

varieties.name: Red Jade

origin.place: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, New York, USA
origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of the German weeping crab 'Exzellenz Thiel'

varieties.history: Raised in the 1930s at Brooklyn Botanic Garden from seed of the weeping crab 'Exzellenz Thiel' and introduced in the early 1950s. Some databases list it as German, probably because its seed parent came from Germany.

look.description: Small, glossy, egg-shaped bright red fruits about 1.5 cm, strung like beads along the hanging branches and lasting well into winter.

taste.summary: An ornamental crab; the small fruit is sharp and mostly left for birds, though it can go into mixed crab jelly.
taste.best_eaten: Not an eating apple; display Sep-Dec

tree.notes: A small weeping tree with a wide, flat-topped crown; usually top-worked on a clear stem. Thin the hanging shoots so the head stays open and sheds rain quickly.

pollination.notes: White blossom from pink buds in spring; its exact flowering group was not found in the sources consulted.

climate.best_climates: Temperate climates of the north-eastern US and north-west Europe, in sunny, airy sites.
climate.poor_climates: Humid, wet districts where leaf diseases can defoliate it.

health.other: Prone to apple scab, with some susceptibility to powdery mildew and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Use it as a focal weeping tree in sun, with a support stake while the head forms. Keep the canopy thinned and clear fallen leaves to reduce scab.

varieties.name: Red James Grieve

origin.place: Seabrook's orchards, Boreham, near Chelmsford, Essex, England
origin.parentage: Sport of James Grieve
origin.raised_by: Found in the orchards of W.P. Seabrook

varieties.history: A redder bud sport of the Scottish apple James Grieve, found around 1922 in W.P. Seabrook's orchards at Boreham in Essex. A separate German red sport (Erich Neumann's Roter James Grieve, 1953) is sometimes also sold as Red James Grieve.

look.description: James Grieve shape and size, but with a much heavier flush and stripes of red over pale yellow.

taste.summary: As James Grieve: very juicy, soft-textured flesh with a lively, refreshing acidity when first picked that mellows to a sweeter balance after a week or two.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct; sharp at picking, softer and sweeter a little later

tree.notes: Tree identical to James Grieve: moderate vigour, reliable heavy crops. Fruit bruises very easily, so handle and store gently.

pollination.notes: As James Grieve: group 3, partly self-fertile and a good pollinator for other mid-season apples.

climate.best_climates: Cool northern climates: Scotland, northern England and northern Europe, where the parent is valued as a reliable early cropper.
climate.poor_climates: In hot summers the soft fruit drops and deteriorates fast; canker is a problem on wet, heavy soils.

health.other: Canker-prone like James Grieve, particularly on wet ground; fairly resistant to mildew. Fruit bruises easily.

varieties.grow_notes: Suits colder and northern gardens where Cox fails. Avoid waterlogged soils because of canker, and pick over several passes as fruit ripens unevenly.

varieties.name: Red Sauce

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.parentage: Deacon Jones x Wealthy

varieties.history: Raised in 1910 at the Geneva station in New York State and introduced in 1926. Its distinction is red-stained flesh that colours the juice and gives a pink sauce when cooked.

look.description: Large conical fruit, largely flushed and striped red over pale green; the flesh is often stained pink to the core.

taste.summary: Coarse, rather dry flesh with a mild, lightly acid flavour; more interesting for its pink colour than its eating quality. Cooks to a rosy sauce.

tree.notes: No reliable growing data recorded.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly late at Brogdale; group estimated from collection flowering dates (borderline 3/4).

climate.best_climates: Bred for New York's cold-winter, cool-autumn conditions; grows in the UK national collection in Kent.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot or very cold regions.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for cooks who want naturally pink apple sauce. Treat as an ordinary mid-season diploid: sunny site, a pollinator in group 3-5, spur pruning.

varieties.name: Red Sentinel

origin.parentage: A selection within Malus x robusta (hybrids of Malus baccata and Malus prunifolia)

varieties.history: A British selection of the hybrid crab group Malus x robusta, valued for clusters of glossy dark red fruit that cling to the branches through winter. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Tiny, glossy, cherry-like fruits about 2 cm, scarlet deepening to dark red, in dense clusters that often last until late winter.

taste.summary: Sharp and not for eating raw; it can be used for jelly, but it is grown mainly for its long winter fruit display and as food for birds.

tree.notes: Vase-shaped to rounded tree reaching about 3-5 m after ten years. Fruit commonly persists into the new year, giving late-winter colour and bird food.

pollination.notes: Plain white blossom early in the season; a good pollinator for early- and mid-flowering apples.

climate.best_climates: Temperate maritime climates like the UK, where the fruit can hang on the tree all winter.
climate.poor_climates: Little information outside the UK; early flowering may be frosted in cold hollows.

health.other: Rated as having good overall disease resistance; foliage and fruit usually stay clean in Britain.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in full sun on any well-drained soil; it needs only light pruning. Useful as a pollinator for early-flowering apples while adding winter interest.

varieties.name: Red Windsor

origin.parentage: Red-skinned sport of Alkmene (Early Windsor), itself Geheimrat Dr Oldenburg x Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: A redder-skinned mutation of the German apple Alkmene, which is sold in Britain as Early Windsor. Known first as Red Alkmene, it was renamed Red Windsor in 1998 and has an RHS Award of Garden Merit; it has also been marketed in supermarkets as Sweet Lilibet. Where and by whom the sport was found is not well documented.

look.description: Medium apple largely covered in bright red, with faint Cox-like striping and a little russet showing through.

taste.summary: Crisp, very juicy, firm yellowish flesh with an aromatic, Cox-like flavour that is tangier and cleaner-tasting than Cox; most tasters find it refreshingly sharp, and it gains a honeyed sweetness only when fully ripe. A short keeper, best eaten within a week or so of picking.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Oct, within a few weeks of picking

tree.notes: Moderate vigour and a reliable, regular cropper; popular for small gardens and containers.

pollination.notes: Early flowering and reported to be self-fertile or partly so; crops better with an early partner. Blossom is vulnerable to frost.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild British and northern European gardens, including the north and Scotland where it is widely planted.
climate.poor_climates: Frost pockets damage its early blossom; hot climates are outside its known range.

health.other: Good scab resistance inherited from Alkmene; early blossom is frost-tender.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy, healthy Cox-style apple for beginners. Avoid frost hollows because it blooms early, and pick when the fruit is fully red and parts easily from the spur; eat soon after.

varieties.name: Redfree

origin.place: Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana (PRI co-operative programme)
origin.parentage: Raritan x PRI 1018-101 (Vf scab resistance from Malus floribunda)

varieties.history: Released in 1981 by the PRI disease-resistance programme, tested as Co-op 13. It was meant as a scab-immune early red apple for home and low-spray growers.

look.description: Glossy, bright red over most of the skin with a yellow-green ground beneath.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy straight from the tree, with a fresh, sweet flavour, a little zing and an overall mild character; some tasters detect an unusual note they put down to its crab-apple ancestry. It softens in storage within a few weeks and opinions vary, one grower finding it soft and flavourless. Dries well.

tree.notes: Average vigour and regular bearing. Fruit ripens over several weeks, so plan more than one picking.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; a good pollinator for others.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates of the US Midwest and East where scab and rust are common.
climate.poor_climates: No clear record of performance in very hot or low-chill climates; a short keeper anywhere.

health.other: Scab-immune (Vf) and very resistant to cedar-apple rust; some resistance to mildew and fire blight.

varieties.grow_notes: Easy, low-maintenance early apple for a sunny garden. Pair with a group 2-4 partner and harvest over several weeks.

varieties.name: Reinette Clochard
varieties.history: A traditional apple of Gâtine in Poitou, originating at Secondigny and widely grown in Deux-Sèvres, Vendée and Charente. INRA Bordeaux crossed it with Golden Delicious in 1958, producing the commercial varieties Chantecler (Belchard) and Charden.

look.description: Medium, somewhat flattened apple with a rough skin, deep yellow when ripe and freckled with small brown russet spots.

taste.summary: Firm, juicy cream flesh with a sweet-sharp balance that leans to the sweet side; it also holds its shape in cooking and gives a sweetish juice. A very long keeper that lasts into March, though it shrivels and softens toward the end of storage.

tree.notes: Upright spur-type tree with short internodes and moderate vigour; crops heavily almost every year, unlike many old varieties.

pollination.notes: Described as late-flowering and so escaping spring frosts, though one French catalogue lists it in early group B. Suggested partners include Reine des Reinettes, Reinette de Caux, Grand'Mère and Chailleux.

climate.best_climates: Mild, sunny Atlantic west of France (Poitou, Vendée, Charente) with warm summers and mild winters.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented in cold continental or very low-chill climates.

health.other: Fairly little troubled by scab; other disease behaviour not recorded. Harvest date for SE England inferred from its late season.

varieties.grow_notes: A regular-cropping keeper suited to a warm, sunny site. Its compact spur habit makes it easy to manage; store fruit cool and humid to delay shrivelling.

varieties.name: Reinette Grise du Canada

origin.place: France; some authors argue for the St Lawrence valley, Quebec
origin.parentage: Unknown; the russeted form of Reinette du Canada

varieties.history: The grey, russeted form of the Reinette du Canada, a large old reinette that French lists date to the early 1800s. Despite the name its Canadian origin is unproven and it has been grown mainly in France, Switzerland and northern Italy, where the Reinette du Canada is still a commercial cooking and eating apple.

look.description: Large, irregular, flattened-round to slightly conical fruit almost wholly covered in cinnamon-brown russet over a greenish-yellow ground.

taste.summary: Fine, dense, lightly crisp flesh, juicy and sweet in the russet manner, with a pleasant sharpness and a distinctly spicy perfume. A mainstay of French cookery: it bakes whole without collapsing, stews to a textured puree that needs little sugar, and keeps a month or two.

tree.notes: Very vigorous with a drooping habit and strong wood; cropping can be irregular. Undemanding of fertiliser.

pollination.notes: Triploid, a poor pollinator; French nurseries put it in flowering group D (mid-late) and suggest Idared, James Grieve or McIntosh as partners.

climate.best_climates: Temperate France, Switzerland and the Alpine valleys of northern Italy, with warm summers and well-drained soil.
climate.poor_climates: Wet sites with heavy soils; triploid vigour makes it unsuitable for very small gardens.

health.other: Resistant to scab but prone to bacterial canker; the Reinette du Canada group is notorious for bitter pit in storage.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it plenty of room or a dwarfing stock, plus two diploid pollinators. Keep calcium and water supply even to limit bitter pit.

varieties.name: Rescue

origin.parentage: Usually given as an open-pollinated seedling of Blushed Calville

varieties.history: A very hardy applecrab selected at the federal experimental farm at Scott, Saskatchewan, and released in the 1930s for prairie gardens where ordinary apples could not survive the winters. It is still recommended for the coldest parts of the Canadian prairies.

look.description: Small, around 3.5-4 cm, yellow-green with a deep red blush and stripes.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy with a tart-sweet balance, good eaten fresh from the tree; it turns mealy within a few weeks. Also used for sauce and preserves.

tree.notes: Tree characteristics not well documented in the sources consulted; valued above all for its winter hardiness.

pollination.notes: Plant with another hardy apple or crab for pollination.

climate.best_climates: Severe continental climates with short summers, such as the Canadian prairies and northern plains.
climate.poor_climates: Warm or hot regions, where an early crab like this ripens in the heat and goes mealy almost immediately (inferred).

health.other: Disease ratings not documented in the sources consulted; main fault is the short life of the ripe fruit.

varieties.grow_notes: A choice for gardens too cold for standard apples. Pick as soon as ripe in August and eat or process quickly; plant another hardy apple or crab nearby for pollination.

varieties.name: Reverend W. Wilks

origin.parentage: Peasgood's Nonsuch x Ribston Pippin

varieties.history: Raised by the Veitch nursery firm, at its Langley grounds, from Peasgood's Nonsuch crossed with Ribston Pippin. It was named after the Rev. William Wilks, then secretary of the RHS and the raiser of the Shirley poppy. It received an RHS Award of Merit in 1904 and a First Class Certificate in 1910, and is still a common garden cooker.

look.description: Very large, broad, slightly conical fruit; smooth pale creamy or milky green-white skin with a light flush and a few soft red stripes.

taste.summary: Crisp, fine-grained, juicy white flesh with a delicate sweet-sharp flavour and a pleasing scent; most tasters find it fine raw, though one found it too bitter to eat uncooked. Cooks quickly to a pale, smooth puree needing little sugar, browns very fast once cut, and keeps only a few weeks unless stored cool and airy.

tree.notes: A stout, dwarfish spur-bearer that crops young and very heavily, but tends to alternate heavy and light years. Thinning in heavy years helps even this out. Well suited to small gardens and trained forms.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering (group 2). Orange Pippin lists it as self-fertile, but it sets better with a group 1-3 partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp temperate climates throughout the UK, including cooler northern gardens, since it ripens early.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are untested. As an early cooker its main risk is short storage rather than a failure to ripen.

health.other: Good general disease resistance (some resistance to scab, canker and mildew). The main faults are biennial bearing, short keeping and fast-browning flesh.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the best early cookers for a small garden or a cordon. Thin heavily in 'on' years to limit biennial cropping, and use or freeze the fruit within a few weeks of picking.

varieties.name: Rhode Island Greening

origin.place: Green's End, near Newport (now Middletown), Rhode Island
origin.raised_by: Attributed to a tavern keeper named Green

varieties.history: One of the oldest American apples, said to have come from a seedling grown around 1650 by a tavern keeper named Green near Newport, Rhode Island. It became a leading 19th-century New York apple, is still grown commercially in the north-eastern US for pies and sauce, and is Rhode Island's state fruit.

look.description: Large, flattish, often ribbed fruit with greasy grass-green skin turning greenish yellow, occasionally a faint orange cheek, and russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Large, hard, firm flesh, less juicy than many, with a clean, strong tartness softened by a little sweetness; tasters pick out cider, grape and lemonade-like citrus hints. Best mellowed in store before eating raw, and at its finest cooked, holding its shape in pies and making excellent sauce.
taste.best_eaten: Cook Oct-Feb; raw after a few months in store

tree.notes: A large, vigorous, spreading tree that is slow to come into bearing and tends to crop biennially. Triploid, so it gives no useful pollen.

pollination.notes: Flowering group 3; triploid, so plant two different diploid pollinators that flower in groups 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Humid continental climates of New England, New York and the Great Lakes, with cold winters and warm summers.
climate.poor_climates: Warm, humid regions with heavy fire blight pressure, and low-chill climates.

health.other: Very susceptible to fire blight; some susceptibility to cedar-apple rust. Triploid.

varieties.grow_notes: Needs plenty of room and two diploid pollinators. Expect to wait several years for the first crops; thin heavy crops to reduce alternate bearing.

varieties.name: Ribston Pippin

origin.place: Ribston Hall, near Knaresborough, Yorkshire, England
origin.parentage: Seedling from pips brought from Rouen, Normandy

varieties.history: Grew from pips sent from Rouen and planted at Ribston Hall in Yorkshire in the early 1700s. It was a celebrated Victorian dessert apple and is almost certainly a parent of Cox's Orange Pippin. It holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Medium, irregular roundish-conical fruit, often lopsided, yellow with an orange-red flush and red streaks over a light network of russet.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained flesh with a strong, aromatic flavour that is more robust, if less refined, than its offspring Cox; sources note a pear-like taste and one grower a pronounced lemon tang. At its best about a month after picking, but it does not stay crisp for long and browns quickly when cut.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Jan; best after a month in store

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous, long-lived spur-bearer. Triploid, so its pollen is of little use to other varieties.

pollination.notes: Generally listed in flowering group 2 (some sources give 3). Triploid: plant two diploid pollinators flowering in groups 1-3.

climate.best_climates: Cool, mild temperate climates across England, from its Yorkshire home to the south, on well-drained soils.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers soften the fruit and dull its flavour; heavy, wet soils encourage canker.

health.other: Prone to canker, especially on wet, heavy soils. Triploid.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on well-drained soil to limit canker, and provide two early-flowering diploid pollinators. Pick in late September and let the fruit mature in store for its best flavour.

varieties.name: Rome Beauty

origin.parentage: Unknown; arose as a shoot from below the graft of a nursery tree bought by Joel Gillett

varieties.history: Joel Gillett noticed an odd tree among grafted stock he had bought around 1816, and his son Alanson planted it beside the Ohio River. First called Gillett's Seedling, it was renamed after Rome Township in the 1830s; the original tree was lost to a flood in 1860. It became one of the main American baking apples of the early 20th century and has given many redder sports.

look.description: Big, smooth, glossy apple with a thick skin, mottled and streaked bright red over a greenish-yellow base, dotted with pale lenticels.

taste.summary: Firm, solid, rather dry flesh with a mild sweetness and a little tartness; unremarkable raw, though one taster found a rose-like note. It shines in the oven, holding its shape when baked whole, and turns dry and mealy if kept long without cold storage.

tree.notes: Bears a good part of its crop on the shoot tips, so avoid heavy tipping-back in winter pruning. Comes into bearing young and crops heavily.

pollination.notes: Late flowering, which helps it miss spring frosts. Often described as partly self-fruitful in North America but crops better with a late-flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Long, warm summers with late springs, as in the Ohio valley, the Virginias and irrigated parts of the US West, where late bloom avoids frost.
climate.poor_climates: Short, cool seasons give small, poorly finished fruit; humid areas with junipers nearby bring heavy cedar-apple rust.

health.other: Very susceptible to cedar-apple rust and also prone to scab, powdery mildew and fire blight; needs a spray programme where these are common.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a sunny, open site and a long season. Prune lightly to renew fruiting wood rather than shortening every shoot, because of its tip-bearing habit. Keep it well away from junipers (red cedar) in North America.

varieties.name: Rosa Mantovana

origin.place: Probably the Kaltern (Caldaro) district, South Tyrol, Italy

varieties.history: An old winter dessert apple of the Adige valley, known in German as Kalterer Böhmer and in Italian as Rosa del Caldaro or Rosa Mantovana. German sources equate the names, but the National Fruit Collection marks Rosa Mantovana as a doubtful synonym, so the identity is not fully settled. In 1929 it supplied over a quarter of South Tyrol's apple deliveries, before newer varieties pushed it out after the 1950s.

look.description: Flattened, somewhat lopsided and ribbed apple, pale greenish-yellow ripening to a waxy yellow, with a bright, unstriped red to carmine flush on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Fine, rather soft white flesh that is sweet with gentle acidity and a delicate, slightly perfumed and mildly winey flavour. Pleasant rather than juicy.

tree.notes: Recorded as upright-growing; little modern information on vigour or cropping.

pollination.notes: Recorded as early flowering in the National Apple Register and at Brogdale (as Rosa del Caldaro).

climate.best_climates: Sunny Alpine valleys such as the Adige around Bolzano and Kaltern, with warm days and cool autumn nights.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented outside its home region.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A heritage choice for collectors of Alpine and Italian apples. It flowers early, so pair it with a group 1-3 partner, and keep the fruit cool until midwinter.

varieties.name: Rosemary Russet
varieties.history: An English russet of unknown parentage, first described in print in 1831 and praised by Robert Hogg later in the century as a dessert apple of the very first rank. It never became as widely planted as Egremont Russet but holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit.

look.description: Tapering, slightly flat-topped fruit, green-yellow with a faint brownish-red cheek and a thin coat of pale brown russet that is heaviest around the eye and the long stalk.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained and juicy, with a lively balance of sugar and acid and a rich, aromatic finish. Sharper than most russets when first picked, it rounds out and sweetens after a few weeks in store.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Feb, after some weeks in store

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous with an upright habit; a regular-bearing spur type that suits restricted forms and standard winter spur pruning.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering (National Fruit Collection records it in bloom with Bramley and Cox); any group 2-4 diploid will pollinate it.

climate.best_climates: Cool to mild temperate climates such as lowland England, where a long autumn lets it build sugar before picking.
climate.poor_climates: Very short, cool seasons may leave it too sharp; in hot humid regions disease pressure and early softening are likely problems.

health.other: Generally considered a healthy garden tree with some resistance to scab and canker; suitable for low-spray growing.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a garden russet: give it a sunny site on well-drained loam and partner it with a mid-season pollinator such as Cox, Discovery or Sunset. Store picked fruit somewhere cool and slightly humid so the russeted skin does not shrivel too fast.

varieties.name: Ross Nonpareil
varieties.history: An Irish apple recorded in County Meath in 1802. Robertson, a Kilkenny nurseryman, sent it to the Horticultural Society of London and it reached English growers around 1819; Victorian authorities ranked it among the best dessert russets.

look.description: Neat, smallish, evenly rounded fruit almost wholly covered in fine golden-brown russet, with a faint streaky orange-red tint on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp and on the dry side, with plenty of sugar and a rich, aromatic flavour that old writers likened to the fennel-scented Fenouillet apples, giving it a faint anise note.

tree.notes: Nineteenth-century growers found it hardy, free-growing and a reliable cropper on most soils; modern growing data are scarce.

pollination.notes: Blossoms early in National Fruit Collection records, about the same time as Ribston Pippin and Egremont Russet; pair with a group 1-3 partner.

climate.best_climates: Mild, moist maritime climates like Ireland and western Britain, where it originated and was long grown.
climate.poor_climates: Untested in hot or strongly continental climates; an early-flowering tree may also lose blossom to late frosts in exposed sites.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well recorded; older accounts describe a hardy, healthy tree.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant in a sheltered, sunny spot away from frost pockets because it flowers early. It tolerates a wide range of soils; pick in late September or early October and keep the fruit cool to enjoy through midwinter.

varieties.name: Roxbury Russet
varieties.history: Arose in Roxbury in the Massachusetts Bay Colony in the mid-1600s and is generally regarded as the oldest named apple variety raised in what is now the United States. It was valued as a winter keeper and cider apple, and Thomas Jefferson grew it at Monticello.

look.description: Dull greenish-yellow apple heavily patched and netted with grey-brown russet, sometimes with a faint bronze cheek.

taste.summary: Dense, firm yellowish flesh, crunchy but not hard, with a sugary, cider-like sweetness, some tartness and a gentle spiciness milder than Golden Russet's; one taster notes a honeyed aftertaste. Improves after a few weeks in store but can shrivel, and the thick, rough skin is slightly bitter. Makes a sweet juice and cider.

tree.notes: Vigorous, long-lived and hardy. Ploidy unconfirmed (one source lists it as triploid); treat it as a poor pollen donor.

pollination.notes: Needs a pollinator; reported as a poor pollinator of other varieties.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter, warm-summer climates of New England and the northern US, where it keeps through winter.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid southern lowlands, where flesh texture and keeping suffer.

health.other: Reported to be fairly resistant to scab, fire blight and cedar-apple rust; flesh browns quickly when cut.

varieties.grow_notes: A tough, hardy heritage tree for northern orchards. Plant a reliable pollinator, prune lightly to keep fruiting tips, and store the fruit for a month or so before eating or pressing.

varieties.name: Royal Gala

origin.parentage: Colour sport of Gala (Kidd's Orange Red x Golden Delicious)

varieties.history: A redder-skinned bud mutation of Gala, the J. H. Kidd seedling from Greytown in the Wairarapa. It was found on a New Zealand orchard by H. W. Ten Hove and patented in the USA by Stark in 1977 under the name Tenroy; it, and later even redder Gala sports, largely replaced the original Gala in commercial orchards. Apart from colour it behaves like Gala.

look.description: Small-to-medium, neat conical fruit, golden-yellow under heavy bright red streaks and flush; noticeably redder than standard Gala.

taste.summary: Sweet and gentle with little acidity and a light, pleasant aroma; crisp rather than hard, with fine-grained cream flesh. Best in season, as long-stored fruit tastes less sweet and can turn soft; tasters are split between a reliable treat and a dull supermarket staple.
taste.best_eaten: Sep-Nov; at its best within a few weeks of picking

tree.notes: Sets heavy crops of small fruit unless thinned hard; thinning is the main job if you want decent-sized apples. Grows like Gala: moderately vigorous with good branch angles.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering like Gala (group 4); plant with another diploid in groups 3-5. A useful pollinator for many varieties.

climate.best_climates: Very adaptable: sunny temperate regions with warm days and cool autumn nights (New Zealand, Washington, Chile, north Italy) give the best colour and crunch; also crops in milder-winter regions such as South Africa and southern Brazil thanks to a moderate chilling need.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, dull, wet climates produce small, scabby fruit with weak flavour; in very hot regions the fruit softens quickly and colours less well, and humid heat brings leaf and fruit rots.

health.other: Very prone to fire blight and to scab; canker can be a problem in wet UK soils. In warm, humid regions Gala types are badly affected by Glomerella leaf spot and bitter rot. Fruit may split at the stalk.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it full sun and a well-drained, fertile soil, and spray or choose a dry site where scab and canker are common. Thin to one or two fruits per cluster soon after June drop for usable size. Pollinate with any mid-season diploid such as Cox, Discovery or Golden Delicious.

varieties.name: Royal Jubilee

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: Raised by John Graham of Hounslow and first recorded in 1888; the name presumably marks Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee of 1887. George Bunyard & Co. of Maidstone introduced it in 1893. It was valued for flowering very late and cropping regularly, and was later grown in Germany and Russia under translated names.

look.description: Medium, tall, narrow-conical fruit, slightly ribbed at the eye; clear pale lemon-yellow, sometimes with the faintest orange flush.

taste.summary: Firm, yellow, medium-coarse flesh with a moderate sub-acid taste. A sound cooker of no special aroma.

tree.notes: Bunyard describes a very dwarf tree that is extremely fertile and crops regularly, so it suits small gardens. Its late blossom usually escapes spring frosts.

pollination.notes: Very late-flowering. The National Fruit Collection records full bloom about the same time as Edward VII, so group 6 is estimated. Pair it with another late variety such as Edward VII or Court Pendu Plat.

climate.best_climates: Frost-prone temperate sites, such as valley bottoms and cold gardens, where its very late blossom avoids spring frosts.
climate.poor_climates: No record from hot or low-chill regions. Late flowering also makes it hard to pair with common early and mid-season varieties.

health.other: Disease behaviour is not well recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: Choose it for a frost pocket where earlier-flowering apples lose their blossom, but plant a late-flowering partner. Its small size suits bush or cordon growing.

varieties.name: Royal Wilding
varieties.history: A Herefordshire cider apple with no recorded origin; Victorian pomologists noted many large old trees, so it clearly predates the 1800s, and in Somerset it went by the name 'Cadbury'. It is not the same as the 'Devonshire Royal Wilding', an eighteenth-century wilding found near Exeter. Material survives in the Tidnor Wood cider-apple collection.

look.description: Small, ribbed, conical fruit, greenish yellow with a brownish-red cheek and fine speckling; very short stalk.

taste.summary: A bittersweet with woolly, tough, not very juicy flesh. The juice is sweet but rather flat and dark, with little acid and moderate tannin; on its own it lacks flavour but it adds body and strength to blends.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; a late fruit for milling in Nov

tree.notes: Described as hardy, leafy and forming a broad, handsome head, but generally a shy bearer that crops well only in favourable seasons.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not recorded; plant with other cider varieties.

climate.best_climates: The cool, moist Herefordshire and West Country orchard climate, where sunny autumns lift its sugar.
climate.poor_climates: Dull, cool summers give thin juice and light crops; performance in hot or very cold climates is unknown.

health.other: Disease record not documented. Main weakness is shy, season-dependent cropping.

varieties.grow_notes: Best treated as a blending bittersweet in a mixed orchard rather than a main cropper. A warm, sheltered site improves both crop and sugar.

varieties.name: Rubens

origin.parentage: Gala x Elstar

varieties.history: Raised by the Italian nursery consortium CIV near Ferrara from a Gala x Elstar cross of the late 1980s, and released as cultivar Civni under the Rubens trademark. It is grown under licence, mainly in Italy and elsewhere in Europe.

look.description: Medium, slightly conical fruit with orange-red streaks and flush over a yellow ground.

taste.summary: Crisp and juicy with a good blend of sweetness and lively acidity that many describe as almost fizzy; more aromatic than Gala, with some of Elstar's character. Keeps three months or more and is slow to brown when cut. Packaging sometimes promises a banana note, but tasters have not reported finding it.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing. A licensed club variety, rarely offered to gardeners.

pollination.notes: Needs a cross-pollinator; UK flowering group not published.

climate.best_climates: Temperate to warm fruit regions such as the Po valley and Alpine foothills of northern Italy, and sunny parts of western Europe.
climate.poor_climates: Cool, wet regions where its scab-prone parents' weaknesses would show; very hot lowlands give poorer colour.

health.other: Described as having average disease resistance; specific ratings not published. Both parents are scab-susceptible.

varieties.grow_notes: Picks about 10-15 days after Gala, so it fits a late-September slot. Treat like Gala for spraying and thinning, and grow in full sun for colour.

varieties.name: Rubinette

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x probably Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: Raised in the 1960s by the Swiss grower Walter Hauenstein at Rafz, north of Zurich, from Golden Delicious most likely crossed with Cox, and released in the early 1980s (Rafzubin is the trademark name). A redder sport, Rubinette Rosso, also exists.

look.description: Small to medium Golden Delicious-shaped fruit with dull orange-red stripes and flush over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Intense, honeyed, Cox-like flavour with hints of pear-drop and an unusually fine balance of sweet and sharp; crisp, juicy flesh under a thin skin. Often rated above Cox and more consistent from year to year; keeps a month or two.

tree.notes: Weak-growing; fruit stays small unless thinned ruthlessly to a single apple per cluster. A semi-vigorous rootstock such as MM106 helps in gardens.

pollination.notes: Needs a diploid partner in group 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Temperate central and northern Europe; reported to tolerate warmer summers than Cox, so a better Cox-style choice for much of the USA.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, humid climates encourage scab; very hot regions untested.

health.other: Scab-prone like Cox, and also troubled by mildew and aphids; benefits from a spray programme.

varieties.grow_notes: Grow for flavour, not ease. Give it good soil, an open site and a semi-vigorous rootstock, thin hard after June drop, and be ready to manage scab in wet years.

varieties.name: Rubinola

origin.place: Institute of Experimental Botany, Strizovice, Czech Republic
origin.parentage: Prima x Rubin
origin.raised_by: Institute of Experimental Botany (Academy of Sciences), Strizovice

varieties.history: A late 20th-century Czech variety from the Strizovice breeding programme, combining the scab-resistant Prima with the well-flavoured Czech apple Rubin. It carries the Vf scab-resistance gene.

look.description: Rounded fruit with a yellow-orange ground largely covered in red; the skin can feel slightly greasy.

taste.summary: Sweet with balancing acidity and an aromatic, rather complex flavour; one taster picks out elderflower and apple-blossom honey. Cream flesh is crisp but light and juicy, does not brown when cut, and keeps a month or two.

tree.notes: Vigorous when young, calming later, with a pyramidal crown of steep shoots. Partly tip-bearing, so avoid shortening every shoot when pruning.

pollination.notes: Needs a diploid partner in group 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Central European conditions; Czech growers report the best flavour at moderate altitudes. Also grown in the UK and Low Countries.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot or subtropical regions.

health.other: Vf scab resistance (can be overcome by new scab races); good mildew resistance reported in Czech trials.

varieties.grow_notes: A good low-spray choice for organic gardens. Use a dwarfing rootstock and spindle or bush form, and prune lightly in summer, leaving some tip-fruiting shoots.

varieties.name: Saltcote Pippin

origin.parentage: Ribston Pippin or Radford Beauty x unknown (uncertain)

varieties.history: Raised by James Hoad at Rye in East Sussex and first recorded in 1918. It gained a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Merit in 1928; its seed parent is thought to be either Ribston Pippin or Radford Beauty.

look.description: Broad, rounded-conical yellow fruit streaked and flushed with orange-red and almost free of russet.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp cream flesh that is only moderately juicy, with a sweet, pleasantly aromatic flavour.
taste.best_eaten: Eating period not well recorded; picked early October

tree.notes: Little published growing information; manage as a typical spur-bearing English dessert apple until it shows otherwise.

pollination.notes: National Fruit Collection flowering dates fall in the mid-season window with Bramley and Cox; assume it needs a partner.

climate.best_climates: South-east England and comparable mild temperate climates where it was raised.
climate.poor_climates: No record of performance in hot or very cold regions; values here are inferred from its English origin.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A Sussex heritage apple for collectors in southern England. Grow on a reasonable, well-drained soil in full sun with a mid-season pollinator such as Cox or Discovery.

varieties.name: Sam Young
varieties.history: An Irish russet brought to English attention around 1818 by Robertson, the Kilkenny nurseryman who also introduced Ross Nonpareil. Hogg rated it a first-class little dessert apple.

look.description: Small, squat apple largely covered in grey-brown russet over a greenish-yellow skin, with a dull brownish-red cheek on the sunny side.

taste.summary: Firm, rather tough greenish flesh; older descriptions call it sugary and highly flavoured, while modern NFC notes describe a milder, subacid taste.

tree.notes: Growing characteristics are not well documented.

pollination.notes: Flowers fairly early in National Fruit Collection records, close to Ribston Pippin; a group 2 or 3 partner should overlap.

climate.best_climates: Cool, damp maritime climates such as Ireland and western Britain.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot or continental climates; estimates here come from its Irish origin.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for Irish and British heritage collections. Site it away from frost pockets because it blossoms early, and store the small russeted fruit somewhere cool and humid to limit shrivelling.

varieties.name: Sansa

origin.place: Morioka, Iwate Prefecture, Japan (cross made in New Zealand)
origin.parentage: Gala x Akane
origin.raised_by: Morioka fruit research station, in collaboration with New Zealand DSIR

varieties.history: A joint Japanese-New Zealand project: the Gala x Akane cross was made in New Zealand and the seedlings were raised and selected at Morioka in Japan. It was released in 1988 as an early, disease-resistant Gala-type apple.

look.description: Gala-like: yellow ground largely washed and streaked with bright red.

taste.summary: Essentially an early Gala: sweet, juicy and crisp, but with more acidity from Akane to keep it lively. Eat within a week or so of picking; late fruit can turn grainy.

tree.notes: Weak-growing and quick to crop, so avoid very dwarfing rootstocks and thin the fruit to keep the tree growing.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4; average pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Temperate to warm climates with reasonably sunny summers; its disease resistance suits humid regions where scab and rust are a problem.
climate.poor_climates: Cold, short-season areas where the weak tree struggles; no long-keeping value.

health.other: Good general disease resistance (very resistant to mildew and cedar-apple rust, some scab resistance). The main limitation is weak growth.

varieties.grow_notes: Give it a semi-vigorous rootstock and good soil to compensate for its weak growth. A useful low-spray early apple; chill hours are an estimate.

varieties.name: Santana

origin.parentage: Elstar x Priscilla
origin.raised_by: Plant breeding research at Wageningen (now Wageningen University & Research)

varieties.history: Raised at Wageningen in the Netherlands from a 1978 Elstar x Priscilla cross and brought to market in the mid-1990s as a scab-resistant dessert apple. It later attracted attention because many people with apple allergy react less, or not at all, to it.

look.description: Medium to large fruit, green to yellow-green with a strong red flush on the sunny side that ranges from marbled to solid.

taste.summary: A delicately perfumed, vinous apple with a sweet-sharp balance, compared with Spartan; some tasters find hints of rose, lychee or sweet grape. The creamy-yellow flesh is usually called firm rather than crunchy, though one grower found it crunchy and tangier than Cox. Keeps a month or two.

tree.notes: Spur-bearing and a regular cropper. Reports of vigour conflict (one source calls it weak-growing, another strong), so judge rootstock choice on site.

pollination.notes: Listed in flowering group 4; an average pollinator for other varieties.

climate.best_climates: Cool to mild temperate climates of north-west Europe, including wet areas where its scab resistance pays off.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, dry summers that favour powdery mildew and are likely to blunt its delicate flavour.

health.other: Vf scab resistance (from Priscilla) and some canker tolerance, but notably susceptible to powdery mildew. Lower in the allergen Mal d 1 than most apples.

varieties.grow_notes: A good scab-free choice for damp gardens, but watch for mildew and remove infected shoots in spring. Pick in late September and eat within a month or two.

varieties.name: Saturn

origin.place: East Malling Research Station, Kent, England
origin.parentage: PRI 1235-100 (scab-resistant selection) x Starkspur Golden Delicious
origin.raised_by: Dr Frank Alston, East Malling Research Station

varieties.history: A disease-resistant dessert apple bred at East Malling by Frank Alston, selected in 1977 and released to growers in the late 1990s. The scab resistance comes from a Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois (PRI) selection; claims that it descends from Falstaff and Cox are mistaken.

look.description: Smooth, rounded fruit with lime-green to yellow skin mostly covered in a deep red flush.

taste.summary: Firm flesh that snaps cleanly and is very juicy; sweet but balanced by a good dose of acidity, so it tastes properly of apple, with faint perfumed hints. Likened to a supercharged Gala; keeps two to three weeks.

tree.notes: Average vigour, starts cropping young and bears heavily and regularly; bred with organic and low-spray growing in mind.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering; reported as partly self-fertile but crops better with a group 2-4 partner nearby.

climate.best_climates: Damp temperate climates where scab and mildew make conventional varieties hard to grow without spraying, such as western Britain and northern Europe.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to dull the red colour and soften the fruit; little evidence from warm regions.

health.other: Carries Vf-type scab resistance and good mildew resistance; other disease responses are not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: One of the easier modern apples for an unsprayed garden in a wet climate. Plant in full sun with a mid-season pollinator, thin heavy sets so fruit size holds up, and eat within a couple of months of picking.

varieties.name: Schöner aus Nordhausen
varieties.history: Arose at Nordhausen on the southern edge of the Harz before 1850 and was put on the market in 1882. It is still common in central German gardens and roadside orchards, and in the 20th century was for a while passed off under the name 'Hindenburg' as if it were a new find.

look.description: Appearance not reliably documented in the sources consulted.

taste.summary: A tart, finely aromatic late apple, picked in October and keeping in a cool cellar from November to April; it mellows enough in store to eat fresh and is also used in the kitchen.

tree.notes: Grown as a garden and standard orchard tree; dislikes damp sites. Ploidy inferred from its reputation as a good pollen donor.

pollination.notes: Regarded as a good pollinator for other varieties; flowering time not recorded.

climate.best_climates: The fairly dry, continental climate of central Germany (Thuringia, Saxony-Anhalt), on free-draining ground.
climate.poor_climates: Moist, humid sites, where the tree does badly.

health.other: Disease ratings not recorded; its dislike of moist sites suggests fungal problems in wet climates.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on a dry, airy site rather than in a damp hollow. A useful pollen partner in a mixed orchard, and its fruit needs a cool cellar to show its keeping quality.

varieties.name: Scotch Bridget
varieties.history: A Scottish cooking apple described in 1851. It has long been grown in north-west England as well as Scotland, where its hardiness makes it a dependable garden cooker.

look.description: Ribbed, conical apple, greenish-yellow largely covered by an attractive orange-red flush.

taste.summary: Soft, tender white flesh, juicy with a lively acidity. Cooks well, and after a couple of months in store it mellows enough to be eaten raw in the new year.

tree.notes: Average vigour, spur-bearing and regular. Ploidy is given as triploid by Orange Pippin but not confirmed elsewhere.

pollination.notes: Mid-season flowering. If triploid, as listed by Orange Pippin, it is a poor pollen donor and needs two diploid partners.

climate.best_climates: Cool, wet and exposed northern and western British sites, such as Cumbria and southern Scotland.
climate.poor_climates: No documented performance in hot summers; colour and keeping are likely to suffer.

health.other: Valued as a tough tree for wet northern sites; specific disease ratings not recorded.

varieties.grow_notes: A good heritage cooker for gardens in the north and west where softer southern varieties struggle. Provide pollination partners and store the fruit cool to extend its season into January.

varieties.name: Scrumptious

origin.parentage: Starkspur Golden Delicious x Discovery

varieties.history: Raised in the 1980s by Hugh Ermen, a Kent fruit breeder who aimed to give gardeners an early apple with more flavour and better disease resistance than the old earlies. It gained the RHS Award of Garden Merit in 2010, shortly after Ermen's death, and is now one of the most widely planted garden apples in Britain.

look.description: Bright, glossy apple largely flushed cherry-red over pale green-yellow; colour varies with sun and can look stripy on shaded fruit.

taste.summary: Sweet but well balanced by a fresh acidity, with the strawberry hint of its Discovery and Worcester ancestry and sometimes a faint aniseed note. Thin skin and white flesh that snaps cleanly at first but goes soft and floury if left on the tree too long.
taste.best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, within a week or two of picking

tree.notes: Branches tend to bend down under a full crop, so thin fruit and support young limbs. Partial tip-bearer: avoid cutting back every shoot tip. Blossom has good frost resistance.

pollination.notes: Self-fertile, so it will crop alone, though a group 2-4 neighbour improves set.

climate.best_climates: Southern and central England and similar cool maritime gardens; bred specifically for UK home growers.
climate.poor_climates: Growers in damp western Cornwall and Scotland report disappointing flavour and some canker; untested in hot-summer regions.

health.other: Bred for disease resistance and generally rated highly resistant to scab, though leaf scab occurs in wet years. Some susceptibility to canker and bitter pit; early fruit attracts wasps and codling moth.

varieties.grow_notes: An easy self-fertile apple for small gardens and trained forms. Pick slightly early rather than late to keep the crisp texture, and thin heavy crops to protect the branches.

varieties.name: Sekai Ichi

origin.place: Aomori Apple Experiment Station, Aomori, Japan
origin.parentage: Delicious x Golden Delicious

varieties.history: From a 1930 cross of Delicious and Golden Delicious at the Aomori Apple Experiment Station; the seedling first fruited in 1946 and was registered (as Aori 4) in 1974. The popular name, meaning 'world's number one', began as a trial grower's boast about its size, and it is sold mainly as a luxury gift apple in Japan and East Asia.

look.description: Huge round to conical apple, typically 500-800 g and sometimes over 1 kg, yellow-green almost covered in bright red stripes.

taste.summary: Mild and gently sweet with very little acidity and little aroma; the dense flesh is crunchy and very juicy. Prized for size and looks more than intensity.

tree.notes: Top-grade fruit depends on careful thinning and good light; the very largest fruits keep less well.

pollination.notes: Diploid and self-incompatible (S3S9); UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cool northern Japan (Aomori), with a warm summer and a cool, sunny autumn.
climate.poor_climates: Little grown outside Japan; no reliable data from hot or very short-season climates.

health.other: Disease behaviour not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for growers who want giant fruit: thin hard to one fruit per cluster and give the tree full sun. Pick in October and keep cold; plant a mid-season diploid partner.

varieties.name: Self-Fertile Cox

origin.parentage: Induced self-compatible mutant (clone) of Cox's Orange Pippin

varieties.history: A clone of Cox's Orange Pippin that can set fruit with its own pollen. British researchers created self-compatible Cox mutants by irradiation and published the work in the early 1980s, and self-fertile Cox trees have since become a standard garden-centre offering for gardens with room for only one apple. In every other respect it is Cox, and it shares Cox's flavour and its weaknesses.

look.description: Same appearance as Cox: golden-yellow fruit with an orange-red flush and red streaks, with light russet around the stalk.

taste.summary: Tastes like Cox's Orange Pippin: rich and aromatic with honeyed sweetness, floral and pear-drop notes and balancing acidity. Some growers find heavy self-set crops give smaller fruit with slightly less depth.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec; flavour peaks a few weeks after picking

tree.notes: Grows like ordinary Cox, a moderately vigorous spur-bearer. Because it pollinates itself it can set heavily, so thinning fruitlets helps both size and next year's crop.

pollination.notes: Sets fruit without a partner, which is the reason it exists; it will also pollinate, and be pollinated by, other group 2-4 diploids.

climate.best_climates: Cool, fairly dry temperate climates like south-east England, the Low Countries and New Zealand's cooler districts, the conditions where Cox does best.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give poorly coloured, soft fruit; wet, mild regions bring heavy scab and canker pressure; very cold winters are also a risk.

health.other: Has the same weaknesses as Cox: canker on heavy or wet soils, plus scab and mildew; it needs good air movement and attentive care.

varieties.grow_notes: Meant for small gardens with room for only one tree. Give it a warm, sunny, sheltered spot on well-drained soil (it hates waterlogging), cut out canker promptly and thin the crop in June.

varieties.name: Sheepnose
varieties.history: Sheepnose is the common rural name, especially in Vermont and Pennsylvania, for the apple pomologists call Black Gilliflower, an eighteenth-century New England variety probably from Connecticut. The southern Crow's Egg is widely thought to be the same apple. Named for its long, tapering, nose-like shape.

look.description: Distinctive tall, tapering, ribbed fruit with dark red skin deepening to almost black-purple, with faint darker stripes.

taste.summary: Greenish-white, firm flesh that is sweet and mild, with a distinctive perfume and a dry, nutty character. Opinion is split: some find it crisp and fragrant, others dry and cardboard-like with little juice. It hangs late on the tree but turns dry and fibrous if over-ripe or stored, so use it fairly soon; traditionally baked or dried.

tree.notes: Spur-bearing and reported to crop prolifically; fruit hangs well but must not be left to over-ripen.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter New England and northern Mid-Atlantic climates, where it is regarded as a hardy variety.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid climates are likely to give poorer colour and quicker drying out of the flesh; inferred from origin.

health.other: Main fault is flesh that becomes dry and mealy if picked late or stored too long.

varieties.grow_notes: Hardy and productive in cold-winter areas. Pick promptly when coloured and use for baking, drying and early-winter eating rather than long storage.

varieties.name: Sheep's Nose

origin.place: Somerset and the West Country, England

varieties.history: The name has been given to several different apples. Hogg (1884) described a Somerset cider and cooking apple called Sheep's Nose, and slightly later writers found it grown in Somerset, Gloucestershire and Worcestershire; the National Apple Register lists four different 'Sheep's Nose' apples, and the American 'Sheepnose' (Black Gilliflower) is unrelated. Which of these is in today's cider orchards is not certain.

look.description: Tall, angular, conical fruit narrowing to a waist and ending in knobbly ridges at the crown; bright crimson broken by yellow stripes.

taste.summary: Hogg's Somerset apple has tender, juicy, sweet flesh with mild acidity, good for cooking and cider; the 'Sheep's Nose' held at the National Fruit Collection is harder, drier and subacid. No cider classification is documented.

tree.notes: Not documented.

pollination.notes: Not recorded for the cider form.

climate.best_climates: West Country and Severn-valley orchard conditions where it was traditionally grown.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: Not documented.

varieties.grow_notes: Check the source before buying: several unrelated apples share this name. Treat it as a mid-season dual-purpose cooking and cider apple.

varieties.name: Shenandoah

origin.parentage: Winesap x Opalescent
origin.raised_by: R. C. Moore, Virginia Polytechnic Institute

varieties.history: Bred in 1942 by R. C. Moore at Virginia Polytechnic Institute from Winesap and Opalescent, and released in 1967. Named for Virginia's apple-growing Shenandoah Valley.

look.description: Large, rounded-conical apple with a mottled and striped orange-red flush over yellow.

taste.summary: Sweet, lightly perfumed yellowish flesh; versatile in the kitchen, where slices hold their shape, but not outstanding raw. Sources differ on texture, some calling it crisp and juicy and Orange Pippin slightly dry. Compared with Kidd's Orange Red but without its richness; keeps three months or more.

tree.notes: A fairly vigorous, vase-shaped spur-bearer that starts cropping young and crops heavily.

pollination.notes: Needs a diploid partner in group 2-4.

climate.best_climates: Bred for the warm-summer, cold-winter conditions of Virginia and the mid-Atlantic uplands; also fruits in the UK national collection.
climate.poor_climates: Very cold northern winters are probably beyond it; untested in subtropical regions.

health.other: General disease resistance reported as good, with some fire blight tolerance.

varieties.grow_notes: A useful dual-purpose apple where summers are warm. Plant in full sun with a mid-season pollinator and allow room for a fairly vigorous tree.

varieties.name: Shinano Sweet

origin.place: Nagano Prefectural Fruit Tree Experiment Station, Nagano, Japan
origin.parentage: Fuji x Tsugaru
origin.raised_by: Nagano Prefectural Fruit Tree Experiment Station

varieties.history: Bred in Nagano from a 1978 cross of Fuji with Tsugaru and released in 1996; the name joins the old province name Shinano with 'sweet'. With Shinano Gold and Akibae it is one of the Nagano 'apple brothers'.

look.description: Large round apple of about 300-400 g, coloured red to deep red in stripes.

taste.summary: Very sweet and juicy with little acidity and a pleasant scent; crisp at first but softer-fleshed than Fuji.

tree.notes: Little published growing data from outside Japan.

pollination.notes: Diploid and self-sterile; UK flowering group not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Central Japanese uplands like Nagano, with warm days and cool autumn nights.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented outside Japan.

health.other: Not well documented outside Japan.

varieties.grow_notes: An experimental choice for UK gardens: give it full sun and a mid-season diploid partner, pick in mid October and expect about two months' keeping in a fridge.

varieties.name: Siberian Crab

origin.place: Wild across Siberia, Mongolia, northern China and Korea
origin.parentage: Wild species (Malus baccata)

varieties.history: The wild crab apple of north-east Asia and one of the hardiest of all Malus. It is a parent or ancestor of many cold-hardy crabs and applecrabs, Dolgo among them, and has been used as a rootstock; the name is also applied loosely to assorted small-fruited hybrid crabs.

look.description: Very small, cherry-like fruits about 1 cm, red to orange-red (yellow in some seedlings), on long stalks in dense clusters.

taste.summary: Small, sharp and somewhat astringent; one grower notes a fleeting sweet, rosy start followed by a dry, bitter finish. Cooks to a pink-tinged sauce and makes good jelly.

tree.notes: Wild trees can become large (10 m or more) with arching branches, though nursery-grown trees on dwarfing stocks stay much smaller. Seedling-raised trees vary in fruit colour and size.

pollination.notes: Early, fragrant white blossom with plenty of pollen; a good pollinator for early-flowering apples.

climate.best_climates: Severe continental climates: Siberia, the Canadian prairies, the northern plains and Scandinavia.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid summers; in mild maritime climates its early blossom can be caught by late frosts after false springs.

health.other: Extremely cold-hardy and generally rated as having good disease resistance, scab included.

varieties.grow_notes: Ideal for very cold, exposed gardens and as an early pollinator. Choose a grafted named tree if you want predictable size and fruit; seedlings vary.

varieties.name: Signe Tillisch

origin.raised_by: Tillisch (per C. Matthiesen); Swedish sources credit Count A. Rantzau of Rosenvold

varieties.history: Danish pomologist C. Matthiesen recorded it as an 1866 seedling raised by Tillisch near Horsens and named after his daughter, though a Swedish account credits Count Rantzau at Rosenvold. It was distributed from Matthiesen's nursery at Korsør from 1889 and became popular across Scandinavia; the original tree fell in a 1975 storm.

look.description: Large, ribbed Calville-type apple with mostly greenish to pale yellow skin.

taste.summary: Juicy, sweet and only mildly acidic, with the soft, tender texture of the Calville group; best for a few weeks in late autumn.

tree.notes: Tree habit not well recorded; scab control is the main task.

pollination.notes: S-alleles S8S34; Scandinavian sources list Cortland, Cox's Orange Pippin and Ingrid Marie among suitable partners.

climate.best_climates: Cool Scandinavian climates; grown in Swedish zones I-IV and widely in Denmark and Norway.
climate.poor_climates: Wet, scab-prone districts; no evidence of performance in hot regions.

health.other: Very susceptible to scab; moderately prone to canker and powdery mildew.

varieties.grow_notes: Plant on an open, breezy site where leaves dry quickly, and clear fallen leaves to cut scab. Needs a compatible pollinator such as Cox or Ingrid Marie.

varieties.name: Sima Joon

origin.parentage: Open-pollinated seedling of Rajka

varieties.history: A late red apple from Karim Habibi's seedling programme at Keepers Nursery, named after his mother Sima and introduced in 2023. The raiser ranks it just behind Primrose Pippin among his selections, and notes it is the better looking of the two.

look.description: Large red-skinned apple.

taste.summary: A crisp late apple whose flavour is described as an even balance of sweetness and acidity. Early reports only; it has had very little independent tasting.

tree.notes: No growing data found.

pollination.notes: Unknown.

climate.best_climates: Only trialled in Kent so far.
climate.poor_climates: Not yet known.

health.other: Unknown.

varieties.grow_notes: No independent growing advice available; ask the supplying nursery for its experience with the tree.

varieties.name: Sir Prize

origin.parentage: Golden Delicious x PRI 14-152 (a PRI selection carrying Vf scab resistance)

varieties.history: Released by the PRI disease-resistance programme in 1975, unusually as a triploid. Its extremely thin, easily bruised skin kept it out of commercial trade, so it survives mainly in home and collectors' orchards.

look.description: Large greenish-yellow apple in the Golden Delicious style, with a very thin, tender skin that marks at a touch.

taste.summary: Tender, very juicy cream flesh with a very sweet, scented, Golden Delicious-type flavour. Good fresh and excellent for baking, but the very thin skin bruises badly in handling.
taste.best_eaten: Autumn, soon after picking (exact timing not recorded for the UK)

tree.notes: Few growing details published. Handle the fruit with great care at harvest because of the delicate skin.

pollination.notes: Triploid and a poor pollen donor; needs two diploid partners nearby.

climate.best_climates: Raised for the US Midwest; probably suits similar climates to Golden Delicious, though this is not well documented.
climate.poor_climates: Not recorded.

health.other: Bred for Vf scab immunity; other disease ratings not found. Severe bruising of the thin skin is the main drawback.

varieties.grow_notes: A curiosity for a home orchard rather than a production apple. Plant with two reliable diploid pollinators and pick and store gently.

varieties.name: Slack Ma Girdle

origin.parentage: Unknown

varieties.history: A long-established sweet cider apple of the West Country, associated with Devon and also grown in Somerset and Dorset. The comic name is variously explained as a warning about its laxative effect or about the potency of its cider.

look.description: Medium, flattish fruit, yellow-green with bright red streaks.

taste.summary: Very sweet, soft and tender with little acid or tannin; pleasant to eat fresh and used in cider to add sugar, with some makers noting a woody note.
taste.best_eaten: Late Oct-Nov, straight from the tree.

tree.notes: A vigorous tree; detailed growth data are scarce.

pollination.notes: Flowering time not reliably recorded.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp South West England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; as a late variety it needs a long season.

health.other: No reliable disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: A good choice for a traditional orchard on a vigorous rootstock. Blend its sweet juice with bittersharps or bittersweets, as alone it makes a thin cider.

varieties.name: Smokehouse

origin.place: Mill Creek, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, USA
origin.parentage: Said to be a seedling of Vandevere; not confirmed

varieties.history: Arose in the 1830s on William Gibbons' farm near Mill Creek in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, from a tree growing beside his smokehouse, which gave it its name. It spread through Pennsylvania and the Mid-Atlantic as an all-purpose farm apple.

look.description: Fairly large, flattish fruit, greenish-yellow shaded and striped with red.

taste.summary: Crisp, moderately fine-grained yellowish flesh with a sweet, honeyed, fresh-cider flavour balanced by some sharpness; some tasters find it almost candy-sweet, and individual fruit can be soft or dry. Keeps well through March and is very good for pies, crisps and drying.

tree.notes: Spur-bearing; other tree characteristics are not well documented.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded; provide a pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Mid-Atlantic and lower Northeast climates with cold winters and warm summers, like south-east Pennsylvania.
climate.poor_climates: Not well documented; climate values are inferred from its region of origin.

health.other: Disease susceptibility not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A dependable dual-purpose farmstead apple for cold-winter, warm-summer regions. Plant with a pollinator and use the fruit for eating and baking through early winter.

varieties.name: Snowsweet

origin.parentage: Sharon x Connell Red

varieties.history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 2006 from a cross of Sharon and Connell Red. The name refers to its very white flesh, which stays unbrowned for a long time after cutting.

look.description: Large apple with a bronzed red flush over a greenish ground; the flesh inside is strikingly white.

taste.summary: Sweet, with just enough tartness for balance and a rich, rounded, almost savoury depth. Flesh is crisp-tender and juicy, and slices stay white long after cutting.

tree.notes: Hardy tree bred for northern gardens; growth habit is not distinctive in the sources available.

pollination.notes: No UK flowering group recorded; plant another hardy diploid or crab nearby.

climate.best_climates: Cold Upper Midwest and similar continental climates with cool autumns.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions where colour and texture suffer, and mild-winter areas lacking chill.

health.other: The breeders report good scab resistance and moderate fire blight resistance; other diseases are not well documented.

varieties.grow_notes: A good modern dessert apple for cold gardens and for salads or cheese boards where slow browning matters. Plant in full sun with a hardy pollinator.

varieties.name: Somerset Redstreak

origin.parentage: Unknown; not the same as the seventeenth-century Herefordshire Redstreak

varieties.history: A Somerset bittersweet of the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, unrelated except in name to the famous old Herefordshire Redstreak. It gained a modern profile through single-variety commercial ciders.

look.description: Attractive rounded fruit, bright red stripes over yellow, tough-skinned with a little russet.

taste.summary: A mild-to-medium bittersweet; the greenish-white flesh is sweet and juicy but rubbery and astringent to bite. Its juice gives a soft, fruity cider.
taste.best_eaten: Not for eating; mill Oct, within two or three weeks of picking.

tree.notes: Vigorous, fairly upright tree reported to yield very well.

pollination.notes: Early-to-mid season flowering.

climate.best_climates: Mild, damp South West England.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented.

health.other: No reliable disease data found.

varieties.grow_notes: An early bittersweet, useful for starting the pressing season. Give its vigorous upright growth room on a standard or half-standard.

varieties.name: Sops in Wine
varieties.history: An old English apple named for its red-stained flesh, which looks as if it had been soaked in wine. Hogg called it very ancient, but the name was used loosely for several red-fleshed apples, so the identity is uncertain; the National Fruit Collection holds accessions that ripen a month apart.
